title: Distributed Job Scheduler
text: Python · Distributed systems. A Celery-style job queue that never runs a job's side effects twice, even when workers are killed in the middle of a job. Every product runs work in the background: sending emails, charging cards, generating reports. Workers crash, deploys restart them, networks time out. If the queue retries a half-finished job carelessly, a customer gets two emails or, worse, two charges. Payment companies, e-commerce and banks all have to solve this. How do you make sure a job runs exactly once, even if the worker dies halfway through? A repeated email is annoying; a repeated payment is a refund ticket. I wanted to build that guarantee myself, then try hard to break it. A job platform in the spirit of Celery: jobs run now or on a schedule, retry with backoff, and land in a dead-letter queue when they run out of retries. PostgreSQL is the source of truth, Redis only carries hints, and every worker holds a heartbeated lease with a fencing token, so a crashed or frozen worker can never commit a job twice. The test was never “does it run jobs”. It was: kill a worker every minute for 25 minutes, fail 5% of attempts on purpose, then audit the database for duplicates. A scheduler promotes due jobs, reaps expired leases and re-sends anything Redis lost. There is no leader: every component can run as many copies as you like. Stack: Python 3.12, FastAPI, React, PostgreSQL, Redis Streams, asyncio, TypeScript, Docker. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Distributed-Job-Scheduler

title: Distributed Job Scheduler: design and guarantees
text: Accepted jobs are never lost: Committed before the 2xx. Leases and a reaper recover dead workers; a sweeper recovers lost messages.. No duplicates from client retries: Idempotency-Key plus a unique constraint. Same key, different body: 409.. Exactly-once effects: A fencing token on every write. Side effects commit in the same transaction as the fenced completion.. Scales without a leader: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and conditional updates everywhere..

title: Real-Time Event Streaming
text: Python · WebSockets. A live cricket scoreboard feed where 1,000 clients receive every event exactly once and in order, through crashes and reconnects. Live scores, delivery tracking, stock tickers and chat all push updates to millions of phones at once, and mobile connections drop all the time. During an IPL match, a score that skips a wicket or shows it twice breaks trust faster than one that's a second late. How do you push one update to a thousand screens at once, when some are on fast Wi-Fi and some are on a train? I wanted to find out how to stop one slow phone from holding everyone else back, and how a dropped phone catches up without missing a ball. A live event feed, demoed as a cricket scoreboard. Producers publish events, PostgreSQL stores them in order, and every WebSocket subscriber on any of three servers receives each event exactly once, in order. Then I attacked it: random client drops, killed server instances and killed Redis connections, with 1,000 clients connected and every sequence number audited. Each instance tracks the last sequence number it delivered. Redis is allowed to lose, duplicate or reorder messages: gaps are filled from PostgreSQL and duplicates dropped. Stack: Python 3.12, asyncio, FastAPI, WebSockets, PostgreSQL, Redis pub/sub, React, TypeScript. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Real-Time-Event-Streaming

title: Real-Time Event Streaming: design and guarantees
text: Ordering: Appends lock the stream's row, so sequence numbers are assigned in commit order.. Race-free resume: A reconnecting client is registered before its history replays, and live events are buffered meanwhile.. Backpressure: Every client has a bounded queue. One that falls behind is cut off and resumes from its cursor; nobody else slows down.. One recovery path: Drops, crashes, deploys, slow consumers and gaps all end the same way: reconnect and resume from the cursor..

title: CDC Pipeline
text: Kafka · Debezium · PostgreSQL. Streams every MySQL insert, update and delete through Debezium and Kafka into PostgreSQL, then proves the copy is identical, even after crashes. Companies keep their live database separate from analytics, search and reporting. Nightly copies are always a day stale, and writing to two places from app code slowly drifts apart. Change data capture is how fintech and e-commerce teams keep those copies in sync within milliseconds, without silently getting balances or reports wrong. How do you keep a second copy of a live database in sync within milliseconds, and know it is right instead of hoping? I wanted to stream every change across, crash the pipeline midway, then prove the copy matched row by row. Debezium reads MySQL's binlog and publishes every row change to Kafka. A sink I wrote applies the changes to PostgreSQL idempotently, keyed on primary key and binlog position, and evolves the schema on the fly. At the end of every run it waits for catch-up and compares every table row by row, plus a SHA-256 per table. Each target row stores the binlog position that wrote it, so replaying an old change is a no-op. Stack: MySQL 8.4, Debezium 3.0, Kafka 3.9, Python, PostgreSQL 16, Docker. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/CDC-Pipeline

title: CDC Pipeline: design and guarantees
text: Per-row ordering: Debezium keys by primary key, so each row lives in one partition, handled by one consumer at a time.. Replays are no-ops: ON CONFLICT ... WHERE target.position < incoming.position.. No loss on crash: Commit PostgreSQL first, then the Kafka offset. At-least-once delivery, idempotent apply.. Schema changes without downtime: New columns are added in the same transaction as the data, under an advisory lock..

Run: 1,000,021 changes at 3,100/s, 3 sinks, a column added at 500k, a sink SIGKILLed at 700k. Lag: p50 89 ms, p95 141 ms, p99 183 ms. Verification: All 5 tables identical, row by row and by SHA-256, across 440k rows. Tests: 33 tests, 93% coverage, including kills inside and between commits.

title: E-Commerce Analytics Warehouse
text: dbt · Airflow · Power BI. 100,000 real orders replayed as a live source into a dbt star schema that is tested and reconciled to the cent on every run. Every e-commerce company runs on dashboards fed by a warehouse loaded from the live database. Late updates, crashed loads and customers who change address make those numbers quietly disagree with reality, and business decisions get made on them anyway. Can a dashboard number be trusted to the cent, even when orders arrive late, loads crash halfway and customers move house? I wanted to build the whole path from a live database to a chart, and stop any run whose numbers don't add up. The Olist dataset is a static snapshot, so I built a simulator that replays its own timeline into MySQL: orders arrive, get approved, ship and get delivered, and reviews come in later. A Python loader moves changes into PostgreSQL incrementally, dbt models them into a star schema, Airflow runs it every ten minutes, and every run is tested and reconciled against the source before anyone reads a number. On top of the marts sit a 4-page Power BI report (37 DAX measures, seller drill-through, row-level security by seller state) and an Excel seller workbook built with Power Query, PivotTables and XLOOKUP. Both match the warehouse revenue to the cent. Airflow runs extract → snapshot → dbt run → dbt test → reconcile. A failing test stops the run before anyone reads a bad number. Stack: MySQL 8.4, Python, PostgreSQL 16, dbt, Airflow, Power BI, Excel, Metabase, Docker. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Ecommerce-Analytics-Warehouse

title: E-Commerce Analytics Warehouse: design and guarantees
text: No change is missed: An updated_at watermark with a lookback window that re-reads recent history for late commits.. Reruns are idempotent: MERGE applies only newer versions. A rerun with no new data applies 0 rows.. A crash leaves nothing half-loaded: Data and watermark commit in one transaction. Tested with SIGKILL mid-load.. Orders join the address at purchase time: SCD Type 2 customer snapshots and a point-in-time join..

Finding: Orders 8+ days late average a 1.7 review score, against 4.3 when on time. BI: Power BI report and Excel workbook agree on R$ 15,735,527.03 of non-cancelled revenue.

title: Postgres Tuning on 38M Taxi Trips
text: PostgreSQL · SQL · MySQL. Twelve analytical questions over every 2023 NYC taxi trip, taken from a 488 ms median to 19 ms with exactly the same answers. As tables grow, analysts' queries slow down and dashboards start timing out. The usual fix is a bigger, pricier server. Knowing how partitioning, the right indexes and precomputed views work can make the same hardware answer in milliseconds. How much faster can the same queries get on the same machine, without changing a single answer? Everyone says “just add an index”. I wanted to read the query plans on 38 million real rows and see which changes actually matter, and what each one costs. Every yellow-taxi trip of 2023 (38 million rows, 4.5 GB) loaded into PostgreSQL, and twelve questions an analyst would really ask. Each question ran against a plain table, then a tuned design with partitions, BRIN and covering indexes and materialized views, measured with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and checked to return exactly the same rows. Then the same suite ran on MySQL. Every plan is committed to the repo, so each speed-up can be traced to the exact change in the plan. Stack: PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.4, SQL, Python, Docker. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/NYC-Taxi-Postgres-Tuning

title: Postgres Tuning on 38M Taxi Trips: design and guarantees
text: Partition pruning + BRIN (832 kB): One week of March: 580k pages read down to 12k.. Covering index: Midtown to JFK for a full year: 356 ms to 7.7 ms, index-only, 0 heap fetches.. Materialized view: Revenue per month for the year: 4,959 ms to 25 ms.. Histogram rollup: Exact tip-percentage quartiles: 2,412 ms to 10.8 ms, no 7.9M-row sort..

title: Showtime: Event Ticketing
text: Java · Spring Boot · React. A BookMyShow-style ticketing app with live seat maps, where a seat is never sold twice however many people go for it at once. When a big concert or an IPL final goes on sale, thousands of people click the same seats in the same second. If two of them both get a confirmation, one turns up at the venue to find someone in their seat, and the ticketing company eats the refund and the anger. How do you let thousands of people grab seats at the same moment without ever selling one twice, and still show everyone the seat map changing live? I wanted to build the full app, Java backend to React frontend, and then stampede it. A full ticketing app: browse events, pick seats on a live seat map, hold them for ten minutes, pay, get a booking. Spring Boot with JWT auth and roles on the backend, React and TypeScript on the front. Seats are rows in PostgreSQL. Holding locks them with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so two buyers racing get an instant yes and an instant no. Payment is confirmed by an HMAC-signed webhook, processed exactly once, and every browser on either server sees seats change as they happen. Each API instance LISTENs to PostgreSQL, so a seat taken through one server shows up instantly for buyers connected to the other. Stack: Java 25, Spring Boot 4, PostgreSQL, React, TypeScript, Server-Sent Events, k6, Playwright. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Event-Ticketing-Platform

title: Showtime: Event Ticketing: design and guarantees
text: A seat is never sold twice: Seat status lives on one row with check constraints; holds lock with SKIP LOCKED and never wait.. Holds expire by themselves: An expired hold counts as free everywhere, so correctness never depends on a background job.. Payments confirm exactly once: Webhooks are HMAC-verified and deduplicated by event id in the same transaction as the booking.. Every screen stays live: pg_notify to LISTEN on each instance, then Server-Sent Events to each browser..

title: Cloud-Native Platform
text: Kubernetes · Terraform · Helm. My job queue run the way production runs it: Kubernetes built by Terraform, autoscaled on queue depth, with a node killed mid-run and nothing lost. Most services don't fail in the code, they fail in how they're run: a node dies, traffic spikes, the database runs out of connections at 2 a.m. Platform and SRE teams exist to make that boring, with autoscaling, failover, and alerts that fire before customers notice. My job queue survived killed workers on a laptop. Would it survive a whole machine dying inside a real cluster, while it scaled itself up and down? I wanted to run it the way companies run services, then pull a node out from under it. A five-node Kubernetes cluster created end to end by Terraform, with the job queue packaged as a Helm chart. KEDA scales the workers on Redis stream lag, CloudNativePG runs PostgreSQL with a hot replica, and Prometheus and Grafana track SLOs with burn-rate alerts. The first load test OOM-killed the PostgreSQL primary: ten autoscaled workers each opened up to 20 connections. The replica took over by itself and no job was lost. PgBouncer now keeps connections flat however many workers run. The whole platform builds from nothing with one `make up`, in about 10 minutes. An AWS version of the Terraform (VPC, EKS, ECR) is validated in CI but not applied yet. Stack: Kubernetes, Terraform, Helm, KEDA, CloudNativePG, PgBouncer, Prometheus, Grafana. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Cloud-Native-Platform

title: Cloud-Native Platform: design and guarantees
text: Node loss loses nothing: Worker leases expire and other workers take the jobs over; fencing tokens stop the dead node's writes.. title: Card Fraud Detection
text: LightGBM · MLflow · FastAPI. A fraud model on 590,000 real card transactions, built the way production needs it: tested on the future, priced in dollars, explained per decision. Card fraud is a race against the clock: a bank has milliseconds to approve or stop a payment, and fraud teams can only review a few percent of transactions. Models that look brilliant in a notebook often fall apart in production because they were tested on data from the same weeks they trained on. Why do fraud models that score well in notebooks disappoint in production? I wanted to build one the honest way: train on the past, test on the future, only use labels the bank would actually have by then, and turn scores into decisions that save money. Vesta's IEEE-CIS data: 590,540 real e-commerce card transactions, 3.5% fraud. LightGBM trained on four months, tuned on the fifth, reported on the sixth. Customer features only look at the past, including known fraud counted only once a chargeback could have arrived, 30 days later. Scores go through a calibrated expected-cost rule (review when the expected loss beats the review cost), models are versioned in MLflow with champion/challenger promotion, and a FastAPI service returns every decision with its top five SHAP reasons. The same features are computed twice, vectorised for training and one event at a time for the API; a replay proves they agree on every value. Stack: Python, LightGBM, scikit-learn, Optuna, MLflow, FastAPI, Polars, SHAP. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Fraud-Detection-MLOps

title: Card Fraud Detection: design and guarantees
text: Tested on the future: Train days 1-119, tune 120-151, report 152-182. A random split would have claimed PR-AUC 0.87; the honest number is 0.64.. Only labels you'd have: Past fraud counts only after 30 days. With 7-day labels the model reaches 0.71; with 90 days, 0.57.. Decisions in dollars: Review when p × (amount + fee) > review cost: 68.5% of fraud cost saved, vs 34% for a 0.5 cutoff.. No training/serving skew: 14.2M feature values and 5,000 API scores matched the batch pipeline exactly..

text: PR-AUC on the held-out month (logistic: 0.53): 0.64. of fraud cost saved vs no model: 68.5%. p95 API latency (8 ms with reasons): 1.1 ms. mismatches across 14.2M live vs batch features: 0. Model: Test PR-AUC 0.644, ROC-AUC 0.936; +0.116 over logistic regression (95% CI +0.105 to +0.128). Cost: $540k → $170k on the test month, 9% of transactions reviewed, 85% of fraud dollars caught. Serving: 5,000 HTTP requests: p95 1.1 ms, 8.2 ms with SHAP reasons. Drift: Score PSI stayed under 0.11 while weekly PR-AUC fell from 0.81 to about 0.6: drift metrics alone would miss it.

title: Financial RAG QA
text: RAG · pgvector · LangGraph. Question answering over 57,638 finance answers where every sentence cites its source, and every design choice was measured before it was kept. Companies are putting chatbots on top of their documents, and the costly failure is a confident answer that cites nothing or cites the wrong thing. In finance a made-up number isn't a typo, it's a liability. Does the standard RAG recipe actually work, or do people just assume it does? I wanted to measure every piece against human relevance labels, keep only what helped, and make the model show where each sentence came from. A RAG service over FiQA, a personal-finance Q&A corpus with 648 held-out questions people labelled for relevance. BM25 and dense embeddings in PostgreSQL with pgvector, fused, reranked, and handed to a local LLM that must cite a passage for every sentence. The measurement changed the design: the off-the-shelf reranker made results worse, so I fine-tuned the embedding model on FiQA's training questions and fused the reranker's order with the retriever's instead of replacing it. A LangGraph agent adds a self-check that drops unsupported sentences. Served through FastAPI with streaming answers and as an MCP server, so other AI tools can use it. Stack: Python, PostgreSQL, pgvector, PyTorch, sentence-transformers, LangGraph, FastAPI, Ollama. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Financial-RAG-QA

title: Financial RAG QA: design and guarantees
text: Measured against humans: Every retriever variant scored on 648 human-labelled questions, with paired significance tests.. Kept only what helped: The textbook reranker cut nDCG by 14%; fine-tuning the embedder and fusing ranks added +7% over dense (p < 0.001).. Every sentence cites: Citations are parsed and checked; unsupported sentences are flagged.. Faithfulness, measured: An LLM judge scores whether each sentence is backed by its citation: 69% with BM25, 80% final, 93% with the agent..

title: Product Analytics & A/B Testing
text: BigQuery · dbt · Statistics. Google's GA4 store data modelled in BigQuery, and an A/B testing toolkit tested on thousands of simulated experiments before reading out a real 14M-user one. Product teams ship or kill features on A/B test results. Peek at the dashboard every morning, pick a noisy metric, or miss that the groups weren't comparable, and you'll launch things that do nothing and kill things that work. Can you actually trust an A/B test result? I wanted to build the statistics myself, prove they behave on thousands of fake experiments, and then read out a real one where the obvious answer turned out to be wrong. Google's public GA4 ecommerce export modelled in BigQuery with dbt: sessions, checkout funnel, retention cohorts, channels and products, with tests that reconcile revenue against an independent deduplication of the raw events. Then an experimentation toolkit (SRM checks, power, CUPED, the delta method, sequential tests, doubly robust estimation), validated by simulation on real GA4 users before reading out Criteo's 14-million-user randomised ad experiment. Results are published on an Evidence dashboard and in a Power BI report with a sample-size calculator. The dashboard is a static Evidence site, rebuilt and deployed to GitHub Pages by CI. The same marts and results also feed a 5-page Power BI report. Stack: BigQuery, dbt, SQL, Python, SciPy, scikit-learn, Power BI, Evidence. Code: https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Product-Analytics-AB-Testing

title: Showtime overview: Showtime: event ticketing with live seat maps
text:
[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Event-Ticketing-Platform/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A BookMyShow-style ticketing app built around one promise: **a seat is never sold twice**, however
many people go for it at once. Buyers pick seats on a live seat map, hold them for 10 minutes and
pay through a gateway whose signed webhook confirms the booking. Every browser watching an event
sees seats being taken as it happens, whichever server it is connected to.

**Backend:** Java 25, Spring Boot 4 (Web MVC, Security with JWT, Data JPA, JdbcClient, Validation),
PostgreSQL 17 with Flyway, Server-Sent Events. **Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS,
TanStack Query, React Router, React Hook Form + Zod. **Infra and tests:** Docker Compose (nginx in front
of two API instances), JUnit 5 + Testcontainers, Vitest + MSW, Playwright, k6, GitHub Actions.

title: Showtime overview: How it works
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B1[Browser] & B2[Browser] -->|REST + SSE| N[nginxReact app, least_conn]
    N --> A1[API instance 1] & A2[API instance 2]
    A1 & A2 -->|hold: lock seats SKIP LOCKED,conditional update, NOTIFY| PG[(PostgreSQL)]
    PG -.->|LISTEN seat_changes| A1 & A2
    G[Payment gateway] -->|signed webhook| N
```

title: Showtime overview: How it works
text:
- **Seats are rows.** Each seat's status, hold and booking live on one row with check constraints,
  so a seat can only ever point at one booking.
- **Holding is all or nothing and never waits.** The hold transaction locks the requested seats with
  `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`; a seat another buyer is taking right now is skipped and reported as
  taken. Two buyers racing get an instant yes and an instant no, with no deadlocks.
- **Holds lapse by themselves.** A held seat past its expiry counts as free everywhere, so
  correctness never depends on a background job; a sweeper only tidies up and announces it.
- **Payment confirms via webhook.** Checkout creates one gateway order per hold. The gateway's
  webhook is HMAC-verified and deduplicated by event id inside the same transaction as the booking,
  so retries and concurrent duplicates book once. A payment that arrives after the hold lapsed still
  books if nobody took the seats, and is refunded if somebody did.
- **Live seat maps across instances.** Changes are announced with PostgreSQL `NOTIFY` from inside the
  transaction, so only committed changes are heard. Every instance `LISTEN`s and pushes them to its
  browsers over Server-Sent Events. Each seat has a version, so the browser merges the snapshot and
  live changes correctly in any order.

Reasoning and alternatives: **docs/DESIGN.md**.

title: Showtime design: 1. Requirements
text:
- A seat is sold at most once, under any concurrency, retries or crashes. This is the one rule
  that must never break.
- Buyers get a short exclusive hold (10 minutes) while they pay. Picking seats is all or nothing.
- Payment is confirmed by the gateway (webhook), not by the browser, and is processed exactly
  once although gateways deliver at least once.
- Everyone looking at an event sees seats go as they are taken, within a second, whichever API
  instance they are connected to.
- Runs as several stateless instances behind a load balancer.

title: Showtime design: 2. Architecture
text:
nginx serves the built React app and load-balances `/api` across two Spring Boot instances
(`least_conn`, because live streams are long-lived). PostgreSQL holds all state. There is no
Redis and no message broker: PostgreSQL row locks give the seat guarantee, and PostgreSQL
`LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` carries live changes between instances.

| Package | Job |
|---|---|
| `events` | Events (JPA entity) and seats. `SeatRepository` has every statement that changes a seat. |
| `holds` | Holding and releasing seats; the expiry sweep. |
| `payments` | Checkout (gateway orders), the webhook, and FakePay. |
| `bookings` | Turning a paid order into a booking. |
| `live` | NOTIFY on change, LISTEN per instance, Server-Sent Events to browsers. |
| `auth`, `config` | Accounts, JWTs, security rules. |

JPA is used where it fits (users, events: plain CRUD). Seat, hold and payment state uses
`JdbcClient` with hand-written SQL, because the correctness of those paths is in the exact locking
and conditional statements, which should be visible and reviewable rather than generated.

title: Showtime design: 3. Data model
text:
`seats` has one row per seat per event: `status` (AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED), `hold_id` +
`hold_expires_at` when HELD, `booking_id` when BOOKED, and a `version` that increases on every
change. Check constraints tie the columns together (`status = 'HELD'` exactly when a hold id and
expiry are set; `status = 'BOOKED'` exactly when a booking id is set). A seat row can name only one
booking, so double selling is impossible at the schema level, not just in code.

`holds` records who holds which seats until when. `payment_orders` has one order per hold
(`UNIQUE (hold_id)`). `bookings` has one booking per hold, order and payment (all `UNIQUE`).
`webhook_events` records processed gateway event ids. Money is integer paise.

title: Showtime design: 4. Holding seats
text:
```
BEGIN
  release the buyer's previous ACTIVE hold on this event, if any
  SELECT ... FROM seats WHERE event_id = ? AND label = ANY(?) FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  every requested seat must be returned AND free (AVAILABLE, or HELD with expiry < now)
    otherwise 409 seats_unavailable {taken: [...]}       -- nothing is changed
  INSERT hold; UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', hold_id, hold_expires_at, version = version + 1
  NOTIFY seat_changes
COMMIT
```

**Why `SKIP LOCKED`.** With a plain `FOR UPDATE`, the second of two buyers racing for a seat waits
for the first to commit and then sees it held: correct but slower. And two buyers locking
overlapping sets in different orders (A1 then A2, versus A2 then A1) can deadlock. `SKIP LOCKED`
never waits: a row someone else is changing right now is simply not returned, and a missing row
means "taken". It answers at once and cannot deadlock. The cost is that a seat whose hold is being
*released* at that moment also looks taken for those milliseconds; the buyer can simply retry.

title: Showtime design: 4. Holding seats
text:
**Why not optimistic locking (`@Version`)?** It also prevents double booking, but under a rush most
attempts would read, then fail on write and retry, which is wasted work at exactly the wrong
moment. Pessimistic locks are cheap here because each transaction touches a few rows for
milliseconds.

**Why not Redis for holds?** Redis `SET NX` with TTLs is a common answer, but it creates a second
source of truth that must be kept consistent with the database's bookings. Here the hold is a
column on the same row the booking will later be written to, inside one transaction.

**Expiry needs no job.** Every query treats `HELD` with `hold_expires_at < now` as free. The sweeper
(`@Scheduled`, every 2 s) only flips such rows back to AVAILABLE and announces them. It uses
`SKIP LOCKED` and conditional updates, so it can run on every instance at once, late, or not at all
without affecting correctness. Time comes from an injected `Clock`, never the database's `now()`,
so tests move time instead of sleeping.

title: Showtime design: 5. Paying
text:
1. `POST /api/holds/{id}/checkout` creates the gateway order once per hold (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
   (hold_id) DO NOTHING`), so double clicks and retries get the same order.
2. The buyer pays on the gateway's page. Here that is FakePay; with Razorpay it would be its
   checkout, and the order would come from its Orders API.
3. The gateway calls `POST /api/payments/webhook` with an event id header and an HMAC-SHA256
   signature of the raw body. The signature is checked in constant time before parsing.
4. In one transaction: `INSERT INTO webhook_events (id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. If nothing was
   inserted, this event was already processed and the response is `duplicate`. A concurrent
   duplicate blocks on the unique key until the first transaction commits, then inserts nothing.
5. `BookingService.confirmPayment` locks the order (a second payment for it serialises here), then
   the hold's seats **in label order** (`ORDER BY label FOR UPDATE`; consistent order means no
   deadlocks). Each seat must still be this hold's, or free. If so: seats become BOOKED, a booking
   row is inserted, the order is PAID and the hold CONFIRMED. If someone else got a seat after the
   hold lapsed, the order is REFUNDED instead and the hold's remaining seats are released.

title: Showtime design: 5. Paying
text:
Because the dedupe insert and the booking share a transaction, a crash part way through rolls both
back and the gateway's retry does the work. A failed payment leaves the hold active so the buyer
can retry before it lapses. An amount mismatch is rejected (422) and rolled back, so it is visible
and retried, never silently accepted.

title: Showtime design: 6. Live seat maps
text:
- **Publish:** every seat change ends with `SELECT pg_notify('seat_changes', json)` in the same
  transaction. PostgreSQL delivers notifications only when that transaction commits, so a
  rolled-back hold is never announced (tested). Payloads are chunked under the 8 KB limit.
- **Listen:** each instance keeps one connection in `LISTEN seat_changes` on a dedicated thread and
  passes each notification to `SeatStreamHub`, which writes it to that event's open SSE streams.
- **Missed notifications:** if the listen connection drops, notifications sent meanwhile are lost.
  On reconnect the instance sends `resync` to all its clients, which refetch the seat map.
- **Browser:** `useLiveSeats` fetches the seat map and opens an `EventSource`. Every `hello` (sent
  on each (re)connect) triggers a refetch, which covers anything that happened before the
  subscription. Live changes go into an overlay, and for each seat the snapshot or overlay entry
  with the higher `version` wins. So the two can arrive in any order without a stale state winning.
- **Shutdown:** the hub is a lifecycle bean that stops before the web server's graceful shutdown
  and closes every stream. Open SSE responses are long-running requests; left open, they made
  graceful shutdown wait out its full timeout (found by the test suite hanging on exit). Browsers
  reconnect through nginx to an instance that is still up.

title: Showtime design: 6. Live seat maps
text:
**Why SSE and not WebSockets?** Updates flow one way, server to browser. SSE is plain HTTP: it
passes through nginx with buffering off, reconnects automatically, and needs no protocol code on
the server.

title: Showtime design: 7. Security
text:
- Passwords: bcrypt via Spring Security's delegating encoder. Login compares against a dummy hash
  when the email is unknown, so response time does not reveal which emails have accounts.
- JWT (HS256), issued at login and validated by Spring's OAuth2 resource server; the `roles` claim
  becomes authorities. Only ADMIN can create events. Stateless, so any instance serves any request.
- The browser keeps the JWT in `localStorage`, readable by any script on the page; the token is
  short-lived and no third-party scripts are loaded. The alternative is an HttpOnly cookie, which
  then needs CSRF protection.
- Webhooks: HMAC over the raw body, constant-time comparison, unknown event types ignored.
- A sign-in `next` redirect only accepts same-site paths. nginx does not expose `/actuator`.

title: Showtime design: 8. Failure modes
text:
| Failure | Effect |
|---|---|
| Two buyers press Hold on one seat | One gets it; the other gets 409 with the seat named, at once |
| Buyer never pays | Hold lapses after 10 min; seats are free immediately, the sweeper announces it |
| Webhook delivered twice, or concurrently | One booking; the duplicate returns `duplicate` |
| Crash during webhook processing | Transaction rolls back; the gateway's retry processes it |
| Payment arrives after the hold lapsed | Booked if nobody took the seats, otherwise refunded |
| An API instance restarts | Its streams close; browsers reconnect via nginx and refetch the seat map |
| A listener connection drops | It reconnects and tells its clients to refetch (`resync`) |
| nginx retries a request | Only idempotent ones; a POST (hold, payment) is never re-sent by the proxy |

title: Showtime design: 9. Limits and next steps
text:
- Seats are picked individually; "best available N together" would be a query over the free
  seats of a row.
- One PostgreSQL. Seat locking is per row, so contention is per seat, not per event; at much larger
  scale, partition `seats` by event.
- A real gateway: Razorpay test mode would replace FakePay (Orders API at checkout, webhook signature
  with the dashboard secret); the webhook path stays the same.
- Queue-based waiting room for very large on-sales, so the database sees a controlled arrival rate.

title: Showtime benchmarks: Booking rush: 200 buyers, 60 seconds, one 1,000-seat event
text:
**Reading the numbers.** Most attempts lose because their seats are already gone, and losing is
fast: `SKIP LOCKED` plus one status check, no waiting. Winning holds and full bookings cost more
and have a long tail. They happen mostly in the first seconds, when 200 buyers arrive at once on a
cold JVM, with about 100 concurrent requests per instance against a 20-connection pool. The median shows
the steady state. CI runs a smaller rush (100 buyers, 20 s) and fails the build if the audit finds
any seat sold twice.

title: Showtime benchmarks: Browser end to end (Playwright)
text:
`web/e2e/booking.spec.ts`, two buyers in separate browser contexts whose live streams are on
different API instances. They race for one seat; the winner pays; the loser sees it held, then
booked. Then the loser's instance is restarted and the stream reconnects and keeps updating.
Passed 18 runs out of 18. In a counted batch of 10, the loser was refused by the server (409) 7
times, and 3 times it saw the seat go to the winner live before its own click registered (which
disables the button). The test accepts both as correct; exactly one buyer won every time.

title: Cloud Platform design: 1. Goals
text:
Run jobq, a job queue whose guarantees were already tested in Docker Compose, the way a production
team would: reproducible infrastructure, autoscaling, high availability, monitoring with SLOs. Then
prove the guarantees still hold when the infrastructure fails underneath it.

title: Cloud Platform design: 2. Two Terraform stages
text:
`infra/local/cluster` creates the kind cluster. `infra/local/platform` installs everything inside
it, connecting with the kubeconfig the first stage writes. They are separate applies because a
provider (Helm, Kubernetes) configured from a resource in the *same* configuration can't plan once
that resource must be replaced: changing the node layout failed with "Failed to get RESTMapper
client". HashiCorp's guidance is to split them, and the Makefile runs them in order.

Inside the platform stage, anything whose *kind* doesn't exist before the apply (HTTPRoutes,
before the Gateway API CRDs are installed) goes in a Helm chart rather than `kubernetes_manifest`,
because `kubernetes_manifest` needs the kind to exist at plan time. The Gateway API CRDs themselves
are vendored at a pinned version (v1.6.3) and applied as manifests: as a Helm release they exceeded
the 1 MB limit on Helm's release secret.

Every chart is pinned to an exact version. The local chart's version is bumped on every change,
because the Helm provider only notices a local chart change when its version changes.

title: Cloud Platform design: 3. Node pools
text:
| Pool | Nodes | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| system | 2 | API, schedulers, PostgreSQL primary + replica, PgBouncer, Redis, gateway, monitoring, operators |
| jobs | 2, tainted `dedicated=jobs:NoSchedule` | workers only (they tolerate the taint) |

The taint, rather than a nodeSelector on everything else, keeps every chart (operators, monitoring)
off the jobs nodes without editing each one. So the failure experiment can kill a jobs node and
lose only workers. Workers tolerate `not-ready`/`unreachable` for 15 s instead of the default
5 minutes, so their pods are replaced sooner. In practice jobq recovers the work even sooner, through
its own leases (see BENCHMARKS.md).

title: Cloud Platform design: 4. Autoscaling
text:
- **Workers: KEDA on the Redis stream's consumer-group lag.** jobq workers read with `XREADGROUP
  COUNT  NOACK`, so the stream's lag is precisely work no worker has room for. One
  replica per 32 waiting jobs (a worker's concurrency), 1 to 10 replicas. Scale up at up to 100%
  every 15 s with no stabilisation window; scale down 2 pods every 30 s after 60 s stable, so a
  brief lull doesn't throw away capacity.
- **Why not CPU?** Workers spend their time waiting on I/O; CPU says nothing about the backlog.
- **Why not Prometheus as the trigger?** It works, but adds the scrape interval (15 s) and rule
  evaluation to the reaction time and makes scaling depend on the monitoring stack. KEDA reads Redis
  directly every 5 s.
- **API: HPA on CPU** (2 to 4 replicas), which needs metrics-server (kind doesn't ship it).

title: Cloud Platform design: 5. PostgreSQL: CloudNativePG and PgBouncer
text:
CloudNativePG runs a primary and a streaming replica, on different nodes by pod anti-affinity, and
promotes the replica if the primary dies. The app reads its credentials from the secret the
operator generates.

**The connection fan-out.** The first autoscaling test OOM-killed the primary. Each jobq process
has a connection pool of up to 20; with KEDA at 10 workers plus the API and schedulers, PostgreSQL
passed 100 backends and its 768 MiB limit. Raising the limit only moves the cliff, because each extra
worker can add 20 more connections. So the app now connects through a CloudNativePG `Pooler`:
PgBouncer in **transaction** mode, two instances, 25 server connections each. However many workers
run, PostgreSQL sees a fixed pool (67 backends at peak, including replication and the operator's
own), and memory stays well inside a 1 GiB limit.

Transaction pooling is safe for jobq because every query is a single statement or an explicit
transaction; nothing relies on session state. The two exceptions were handled:
- **Prepared statements:** asyncpg uses named prepared statements, which PgBouncer supports across
  server connections with `max_prepared_statements` set.
- **Migrations** hold a session-level advisory lock, which transaction pooling can't keep, so the
  migrate init containers connect to the primary directly.

title: Cloud Platform design: 6. Monitoring and SLOs
text:
kube-prometheus-stack, with selectors opened so it picks up every ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor and
PrometheusRule in the cluster. The chart ships monitors for the API, schedulers, workers, PostgreSQL
and PgBouncer.

| SLO | Indicator | Objective |
|---|---|---|
| Pickup | job claimed by a worker within 5 s of becoming due (`jobq_queue_delay_seconds`) | 99% |
| Enqueue | API accepts a job within 100 ms (`jobq_enqueue_seconds`) | 99% |

Error ratios are recorded over 5 m, 30 m, 1 h and 6 h windows. Alerts follow the Google SRE
workbook's multi-window, multi-burn-rate method: **page** when both the 1 h and 5 m windows burn the
budget at 14.4× (2% of a 30-day budget in an hour), **ticket** at 6× over 6 h and 30 m. The short
window makes alerts stop soon after the problem does.

**A bug the tests caught:** the first recording rules computed `1 - good / max(total, ε)`, so an
idle queue (no jobs in the window) became a 100% error ratio and kept paging after the load test
ended. They now compute `(total - good) / (total > 0)`: no traffic gives no data, not total failure.
Also alerted: dead letters, workers pinned at the maximum, and a backlog growing for 10 minutes.

title: Cloud Platform design: 7. Security and hardening in the chart
text:
Non-root containers with a read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped and the
`RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile; `enableServiceLinks: false` (see §8); PodDisruptionBudget for the
API; graceful shutdown (workers finish or release their jobs on SIGTERM within 25 s, and the pod
gives them 40 s). Secrets come from the operator, not from values files. The dev API key in
values.yaml is for the local cluster only.

title: Cloud Platform design: 8. Things that went wrong, and why
text:
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every jobq pod failed: `api_port: unable to parse 'tcp://10.96...:8000'` | Kubernetes injects Docker-style variables for every Service; the `jobq-api` Service became `JOBQ_API_PORT`, which jobq reads as its own setting | `enableServiceLinks: false` |
| PostgreSQL primary OOM-killed under load | connection fan-out from autoscaled workers | PgBouncer (transaction pooling), 1 GiB limit |
| Traefik release "failed" although it ran | service type was `LoadBalancer` (wrong values key), and Helm waited for an external IP kind never assigns | `service.spec.type: NodePort` |
| KEDA release failed on a fresh cluster | the operator restarts while issuing webhook certificates, longer than Helm's 5-minute wait | 10-minute timeout |
| Monitoring pods failing with "no space left on device" | Docker VM disk full | pruned caches; Colima disk 40 GB → 80 GB |
| SLO alert firing on an idle system | idle window treated as 100% errors | see §6 |
| Load generator hung after the database crash | requests on dead connections outlived httpx's timeout | hard per-attempt deadline |

title: Cloud Platform benchmarks: Method
text:
`load/experiment.py` runs `load/enqueue.py` inside the cluster as a Kubernetes Job on a system node.
It sends N `examples.ledger` jobs **open loop** at a fixed rate, each with an Idempotency-Key, and
retries through errors. Each job sleeps for its work time, then writes one row to `example_ledger`
in the same transaction as its fenced completion. Every 5 s the runner records the backlog, worker
replicas, jobs in flight, PostgreSQL connections and memory from Prometheus. For failure runs, it
`docker stop`s the jobs node running the most workers: the node simply vanishes, with no drain.

When every job has finished, it audits PostgreSQL: each job must have succeeded and have **exactly
one** ledger row, however many times it ran. Raw timelines and summaries are in `load/results/`.

title: Cloud Platform benchmarks: Results
text:
**What the node failure shows.** Kubernetes reported the dead node's four workers as ready until
about 94 s, some 50 s after the node vanished, because that's how long it takes to declare a node
NotReady. jobq didn't need to wait: those workers' 10-second leases lapsed, the scheduler's reaper
re-queued their 117 jobs, and the surviving workers finished the backlog at 84 s, 16 s later than
without the failure. Writes the dead workers attempted afterwards were fenced (rejected), which
shows on the dashboard's throughput panel as a small "fenced" series. No job's side effect was
committed twice.

**Throughput ceiling.** Ten workers peaked at about 270 completed jobs/s, below the 400/s offered,
so the backlog kept growing until the arrivals stopped. Ten workers of 32 slots at 500 ms each
could in theory do 640/s; on this laptop they share 12 vCPUs with the database, the pooler, the
monitoring stack and the load generator.

**SLOs during the tests.** These runs deliberately offer 6× one worker's capacity, so jobs wait for
scale-out and the pickup SLO (99% within 5 s) is violated. Its fast-burn alert fired (page) and the
slow-burn alert fired (ticket), as designed. The enqueue SLO held: 99.87% of enqueues in the hour
under 100 ms.

title: Cloud Platform benchmarks: The run that crashed the database
text:
The first 20,000-job run (before PgBouncer) passed 100 PostgreSQL connections at 10 workers. The
primary was **OOM-killed** (exit 137) at its 768 MiB limit. CloudNativePG promoted the replica on its
own, and the old primary rejoined as a replica.

| Audit of the jobs accepted before the crash | |
|---|---|
| Jobs accepted | 18,832 |
| Succeeded | 18,832 |
| Ran more than once | 271 |
| Lost / duplicated effects | **0 / 0** |

The load generator itself hung after the crash: requests on connections that died mid-failover
outlived httpx's timeout. That's why only 18,832 of 20,000 were sent. It now has a hard per-attempt
deadline, and the database has a connection pooler (DESIGN.md §5).

title: Job Scheduler overview: jobq: distributed task scheduler and job queue
text:
[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Distributed-Job-Scheduler/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A job platform in the spirit of Celery or Sidekiq, built around **correctness under failure**.
Jobs run now or on a schedule and retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Jobs that exhaust
their retries go to a dead-letter queue. Workers hold heartbeated **leases**, and every write is
**fenced**, so a crashed or frozen worker can never commit a job twice.

It comes with a React dashboard for watching queues, throughput and workers, following any job's
attempts, cancelling, enqueueing, and requeueing dead letters.

**Backend:** Python 3.12, asyncio, FastAPI, PostgreSQL (source of truth), Redis Streams
(dispatch) and Lua (rate limiting), Docker, GitHub Actions.
**Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, React Router, React Hook
Form + Zod; tested with Vitest, Testing Library, MSW and Playwright.

title: Job Scheduler overview: Measured results (details)
text:
| 50,000 jobs at 2,000/min, a worker `SIGKILL`ed every minute, 5% of attempts failing | |
|---|---|
| Unrecovered failures | **0** (50,000 / 50,000 succeeded; 2,633 retries and 41 crash-interrupted jobs recovered) |
| Duplicate side effects | **0** (audited in SQL: one ledger row per job) |
| Enqueue latency | **p95 7.1 ms**, p99 8.2 ms |
| Peak throughput (same laptop) | **≈ 1,500 jobs/s** end-to-end, pickup p95 3.5 ms |
| Dashboard end to end (Playwright, 4 runs) | A worker SIGKILLed mid-run each time: **all 200–500 jobs succeeded with exactly one ledger row each**, and the UI showed the 32 taken-over jobs' `lease_expired` attempt then the success on another worker |

title: Job Scheduler overview: Architecture
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Client SDK / REST] -->|POST /v1/jobs + Idempotency-Key| A[API x NFastAPI]
    A -->|token bucket, Lua| R[(Redis)]
    A -->|INSERT, idempotent| P[(PostgreSQLjobs, executions)]
    A -->|XADD job id| S[[Redis Streamsone per queue]]
    S -->|XREADGROUP NOACK| W[Workers x Nasyncio]
    W -->|claim lease, heartbeat,fenced complete| P
    SC[Scheduler x N] -->|promote due, reap expired leases,sweep lost messages, purge| P
    SC -->|XADD| S
```

**PostgreSQL is the source of truth; Redis only carries hints.** Every state change is a single
conditional `UPDATE` that the database arbitrates. Redis can lose messages, or all of its data,
without losing a job: the scheduler's sweeper notices and dispatches again.

| Guarantee | How |
|---|---|
| Accepted jobs are never lost | Committed before the 2xx; leases + reaper recover dead workers; sweeper recovers lost messages |
| No duplicate jobs from client retries | `Idempotency-Key` + unique constraint; reuse with a different body → 409 |
| At-least-once execution | An expired lease is rescheduled (backoff, or DLQ when the budget is spent) |
| Exactly-once *effects* | Fencing token on every write; `ctx.transactional(sql)` commits side effects in the same transaction as the fenced completion |
| Horizontal scaling, no leader | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and conditional updates everywhere; run any number of each component |

title: Job Scheduler overview: Dashboard
text:
`web/` is a React + TypeScript app that the API serves at `/` (the Docker image builds it).

- **Overview:** job counts by status and queue, throughput over the last 5 minutes (succeeded vs
  failed attempts per 10 s), and the workers that ran your jobs recently, with quiet ones flagged.
  It refreshes every 2 seconds.
- **Jobs:** filter by status, queue and task. The filters live in the URL, so a view can be
  shared. Pages load with "Load more" on the API's keyset cursor.
- **Job:** arguments, result or error, and every attempt in order: which worker ran it, how long
  it took, and why it failed (`lease_expired`, `fenced` and so on, in plain words). A pending job
  can be cancelled after a confirmation step; a dead one can be requeued.
- **Dead letters:** select several or all, requeue them four at a time, with progress and a list
  of any that failed.
- **New job:** a validated form (Zod) with presets for the example tasks. The JSON arguments are
  checked before sending, and each submit carries a fresh `Idempotency-Key`, so a double click
  or a retry cannot create two jobs.

text:
```python
from jobq import JobContext, JobQ, PermanentError, RetryLater

app = JobQ("http://localhost:8000", api_key="jq_...")

@app.task(max_attempts=5, queue="emails", timeout_s=30)
def send_welcome_email(user_id: int) -> str:
    ...

@app.task(bind=True)
async def charge(ctx: JobContext, order_id: int, cents: int) -> None:
    # ctx.idempotency_key is the job id: stable across retries, so the provider dedupes
    await payments.charge(order_id, cents, idempotency_key=ctx.idempotency_key)
    # runs in the same transaction as the fenced completion: commits exactly once
    ctx.transactional("UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = $1", order_id)

result = send_welcome_email.delay(42)                      # run now
send_welcome_email.apply_async(args=[7], countdown=3600)   # run in an hour
result.get(timeout=10)                                     # wait for the return value
```

Workers import the same module: `jobq worker --tasks myapp.tasks --queues default,emails`.
Tasks can `raise RetryLater(30)` to pick their own delay or `raise PermanentError(...)` to skip
straight to the DLQ.

title: Job Scheduler overview: Testing
text:
```bash
make infra   # Postgres + Redis in Docker
make check   # ruff, mypy, 90 tests with coverage gate (94%)
make web-test && make e2e   # dashboard: 38 component tests (99% lines), 2 Playwright tests
```

The tests run against real PostgreSQL and Redis, because the guarantees depend on real row
locking and stream semantics. **`tests/test_chaos.py`** starts real worker processes and:

- **SIGKILLs a worker mid-job.** Its leases expire, the reaper reschedules the jobs and another
  worker finishes them. Each of the 80 jobs has exactly one ledger row.
- **Freezes a worker with SIGSTOP** until its 10 jobs are taken over, then SIGCONTs it. The
  "zombie" finishes all its handlers, but every write is fenced off: still exactly one row per job.

**`web/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts`** does the same through the browser against the compose stack.
It enqueues 200 ledger jobs, finds the worker running the most of them, `docker kill`s its
container, and waits for every job to succeed. Then it counts ledger rows in PostgreSQL (one per
job) and opens a taken-over job in the dashboard to check its `lease_expired` attempt. A second
test enqueues through the form, then dead-letters three jobs and requeues them from the UI.

title: Job Scheduler design: jobq: Design
text:
This document explains *why* jobq is built the way it is. Each section states the problem, the
decision, and the alternatives considered.

title: Job Scheduler design: 1. Requirements
text:
**Functional**
- Submit a job (task name + JSON args) to run now or at/after a time.
- Workers execute jobs; failures retry with exponential backoff; jobs that exhaust their retries
  land in a dead-letter queue (DLQ) that can be inspected and requeued.
- Every attempt is recorded (worker, timing, error): execution history.
- REST API with API-key auth and per-key rate limiting; a Celery-style Python SDK.

**Non-functional**
- **No lost jobs**: once the API returns 2xx, the job will eventually reach a terminal state,
  even if any single process (API, scheduler, worker, Redis) crashes.
- **No duplicate effects**: a job's committed side effects happen once, even when the job itself
  is executed more than once (which at-least-once delivery makes unavoidable).
- **Horizontal scale**: any component can run as N replicas without coordination.
- Low enqueue latency (target p95  [AND lease_token = ]`, so concurrent
  actors race safely: the database decides the winner.
- Redis Streams carry only job ids ("this job is ready") so idle workers block on
  `XREADGROUP` and get work in ~1 ms instead of polling PostgreSQL. If Redis loses messages, or
  loses everything, the scheduler's sweeper notices from PostgreSQL and re-sends them.
- Redis also holds rate-limit buckets, which are disposable by nature.

title: Job Scheduler design: Why not just PostgreSQL (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` polling)?
text:
That design (used by Oban, good_job, pg-boss) is simpler and would work at this scale. Its
costs: every idle worker polls the database (N workers × poll rate queries/s even when idle), and
pickup latency is bounded by the poll interval. Push-based dispatch through Redis gives
~sub-millisecond pickup and zero idle load on PostgreSQL. The scheduler *does* use SKIP LOCKED
for its batch loops, where polling is cheap (one query per interval, not per worker).

title: Job Scheduler design: Why not Redis as the source of truth (like Celery/RQ/Sidekiq)?
text:
Redis persistence is asynchronous (AOF `everysec` can lose ~1 s of writes; failover can lose
more), and it cannot express "update this job only if I still hold the lease" together with
"and insert my side effect" atomically with the business data. Keeping truth in PostgreSQL gives
durability, transactions, secondary indexes for the API (list/filter/paginate), and SQL for
audits (the benchmark verifies exactly-once with one query).

title: Job Scheduler design: Why not Kafka / SQS?
text:
Kafka is a log, not a job queue: per-message acks, delays, retries with backoff and a DLQ all have
to be built on top, and partition-level ordering limits parallelism to the partition count. SQS
gives visibility timeouts (≈ leases) and DLQs, but has no fencing (a slow consumer can still act
after its message reappeared), limited delays (15 min), and nothing to query history. jobq
implements the same ideas explicitly so each one can be explained and tested.

title: Job Scheduler design: 3. Data model
text:
`jobs` (one row per job): `status`, `run_at`, `attempts`, `max_attempts`, `attempt_offset`,
backoff parameters, lease (`lease_token`, `lease_owner`, `lease_expires_at`), `dispatched_at`,
`result`, `last_error`, `idempotency_key` + `request_hash`, timestamps.

`executions` (one row per attempt): `attempt`, `worker_id`, `lease_token`, `status`
(`running|succeeded|failed|timed_out|lease_expired|fenced|interrupted`), `error`, timings.
`UNIQUE (job_id, attempt)`.

**Partial indexes.** Each background loop only touches rows in one state, so each gets an index
over just those rows: `(run_at) WHERE status='scheduled'`, `(lease_expires_at) WHERE
status='running'`, `(dispatched_at) WHERE status='queued'`. These stay tiny even when the table
holds millions of finished jobs, so loop queries stay O(batch).

**Vacuum.** A queue table is update-heavy (each job is updated ~3-5 times), producing dead tuples
quickly. Autovacuum thresholds are lowered for `jobs` (2% instead of 20%) to prevent bloat.

title: Job Scheduler design: 4. Job state machine
text:
```
                 delay/run_at in future
   POST /jobs ──────────────────────────▶ scheduled ──(run_at ≤ now: promoter)──┐
       │ due now                              ▲  ▲                             │
       ▼                                      │  │ retry with backoff          ▼
    queued ◀───────────── DLQ requeue ─────┐  │  │ (failure / lease expiry)  queued
       │  worker claim (conditional UPDATE)│  │  │
       ▼                                   │  │  │
    running ──success (fenced)──▶ succeeded│  │  │
       │ │                                 │  │  │
       │ └─failure, budget left────────────┼──┘  │
       │   failure, budget spent / Permanent ▶ dead
       └─lease expired (reaper)──────────────────┘
    scheduled|queued ──POST cancel──▶ cancelled
```

title: Job Scheduler design: 5.1 Enqueue (API)
text:
1. Authenticate (in-process cache → `api_keys` lookup by prefix → constant-time hash compare).
2. Rate-limit: Lua token bucket in Redis (atomic; uses Redis's clock so API replicas agree).
3. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (api_key_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING *`. The status is
   computed in SQL: `queued` if `run_at  BLOCK 1000 NOACK`. A worker only reads as many messages as it
  has free concurrency slots, so it never hoards work that other workers could run.
- **Claim** in one statement (a data-modifying CTE also opens the execution row):
  `UPDATE jobs SET status='running', attempts=attempts+1, lease_token=$new_uuid,
  lease_expires_at=now()+lease WHERE id=$1 AND status='queued'`. Zero rows → someone else has it
  (or it was cancelled, or this was a duplicate message): drop it.
- **Run** the handler under `asyncio.timeout(timeout_s)`. Sync handlers run in a thread.
- **Heartbeat**: one query per worker per interval extends *all* its leases
  (`UPDATE ... FROM unnest($ids, $tokens)`), instead of one query per job. Any job missing from
  the result has lost its lease → its handler is cancelled immediately.
- **Complete** with fencing: `UPDATE ... SET status='succeeded' WHERE id=$1 AND
  lease_token=$mine AND status='running'`; the task's transactional side effects run in the same
  transaction, after this check passes.
- **Fail**: `decide_failure()` → `scheduled` with `run_at = now() + backoff` or `dead`. Also fenced.

title: Job Scheduler design: 5.1 Enqueue (API)
text:
Timestamps for leases always come from PostgreSQL's `now()`, never worker clocks, so clock skew
between worker hosts cannot make a lease look valid or expired incorrectly.

title: Job Scheduler design: 5.4 Reap (scheduler)
text:
Jobs `running` with `lease_expires_at  30 s", which would flood the stream with duplicates exactly when the system
is already behind. Lost jobs get `dispatched_at = now()` and a fresh XADD; if two sweepers race,
the worst case is a duplicate message, which the conditional claim makes harmless.

title: Job Scheduler design: 5.6 Graceful shutdown (worker)
text:
SIGTERM → stop reading → wait up to `shutdown_grace_s` for in-flight jobs → cancel the rest and
**release** them (`scheduled`, `run_at = now()`, `attempt_offset += 1` so the interrupted attempt
does not consume retry budget; execution `interrupted`) → remove the consumer from the group.

title: Job Scheduler design: 6. Delivery guarantees
text:
| Property | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Durability of accepted jobs | Committed to PostgreSQL before the API responds |
| No lost jobs | Leases + reaper (worker death), sweeper (lost messages), commit-before-dispatch |
| At-least-once execution | A job whose worker vanished is re-run after its lease expires |
| At-most-once *commit* | Fencing token (`lease_token`) on every completion write |
| Exactly-once *effects* | `ctx.transactional(sql)` runs in the completion transaction; for external APIs pass `ctx.idempotency_key` (the job id) downstream |
| No duplicate jobs from retries | `Idempotency-Key` + unique constraint + request-hash check |

"Exactly-once delivery" is impossible in a distributed system with failures (the two-generals
problem): if a worker completes the work and dies before recording it, *someone* has to decide
whether to run it again. jobq chooses to re-run (at-least-once) and makes the effect idempotent.

title: Job Scheduler design: Why fencing tokens matter
text:
Leases alone are not enough. A worker can stall *longer than its lease* (GC pause, VM
suspension, network partition) and then wake up still believing it owns the job, while another
worker has already taken over. Without a fence, both would write results. (This is the argument
from Martin Kleppmann's "How to do distributed locking".) Here the fence is the random
`lease_token` checked on every write. `tests/test_chaos.py` reproduces it with real processes:
it `SIGSTOP`s a worker holding 10 jobs until the reaper hands them to another worker, then
`SIGCONT`s it. The zombie finishes all 10 handlers, and none of its writes land.

title: Job Scheduler design: 7. Failure modes
text:
| Failure | What happens | Recovery time |
|---|---|---|
| Worker SIGKILL / OOM / host loss | Leases expire; reaper reschedules (counts as an attempt) | `lease_s` + reap interval |
| Worker stalls (GC, partition) | Same; its late writes are fenced | same |
| Worker dies between read and claim | Message lost (NOACK); sweeper re-sends | `sweep_after_s` |
| Scheduler dies | Other replicas continue (no leader); otherwise loops resume on restart | 0 with ≥2 replicas |
| API dies mid-request | Client retries with the same Idempotency-Key → at most one job | client retry |
| Redis down | Enqueue still succeeds (dispatch skipped, rate limiter fails open); workers back off and reconnect; sweeper re-dispatches | Redis downtime + `sweep_after_s` |
| Redis loses all data | Workers recreate groups on `NOGROUP`; sweeper re-sends every queued job | `sweep_after_s` |
| PostgreSQL down | API returns 5xx (nothing accepted that could be lost); workers retry status writes, then leases expire and jobs re-run | PG downtime + `lease_s` |
| Handler hangs | `timeout_s` fails the attempt (thread-based sync handlers keep running in the background, but their transactional effects can no longer commit) | `timeout_s` |
| Poison job | Retries with backoff until `max_attempts`, then DLQ; `PermanentError` skips retries | bounded |

title: Job Scheduler design: 8. Retry policy
text:
Exponential backoff with **full jitter**: `delay = uniform(0, min(max, base · 2^(n−1)))`. Without
jitter, jobs that failed together (a dependency outage) retry together and cause synchronized
load spikes; full jitter spreads them (AWS Architecture Blog, "Exponential Backoff And Jitter").
Tasks can override the delay (`raise RetryLater(30)`) or skip retries (`raise PermanentError`).
Unknown task names are retryable on purpose: during a rolling deploy, a newer worker may know it.

title: Job Scheduler design: 9. Security
text:
- API keys `jq__`: the prefix is an indexed lookup key; only
  `sha256(secret)` is stored. A fast hash is correct here, unlike passwords: the secret has 256
  bits of entropy, so brute force is infeasible and bcrypt would only add latency to every request.
  Compared with `hmac.compare_digest` (constant time). Keys can be revoked; the verification cache
  TTL (default 30 s) bounds how long a revoked key still works.
- Tenant isolation: every query filters on `api_key_id`; another tenant's job returns 404, not
  403, so ids cannot be probed.
- Payload size limit (256 KiB, 413), strict validation of names/queues, non-root container.

title: Job Scheduler design: 10. The dashboard
text:
A React + TypeScript single-page app in `web/`, built into the Python package and served by the
API at `/`. A catch-all route registered after every API route returns the page for client-side
paths, and returns 404 for unknown `/v1/` paths, so a typo in an API call never gets HTML back.

title: Job Scheduler design: 10. The dashboard
text:
- **Polling, not push.** Counts, throughput and job state change continuously, but nobody needs
  them within milliseconds. TanStack Query polls every 2 s (1 s on a pending job's page, stopping
  once it is terminal), deduplicates requests and refetches when the tab regains focus. Push
  (SSE from a PostgreSQL `LISTEN`) would be the next step if many people watched one deployment.
- **Two endpoints for it.** `GET /v1/workers` and `GET /v1/stats/throughput` read only recent or
  running executions. Migration 0003 indexes `executions (started_at)` and running executions
  for that. Both are scoped to the caller's key like every other query.
- **Auth.** The dashboard uses the same API keys as the SDK. The key is checked with a request
  before it is kept, stored in `sessionStorage` (gone when the tab closes) and sent only as the
  `X-API-Key` header to the same origin. A 401 signs the user out with the reason. Each signed-in
  key gets its own query cache, so data never leaks between keys. Script injected into the page
  could read the key; the API's per-key rate limits and revocation limit the damage, and a
  production deployment would use short-lived session tokens in an `HttpOnly` cookie instead.
- **Rendering stays pure.** "5 s ago" and "stale worker" are computed against each query's
  fetch time (`dataUpdatedAt`), not `Date.now()`, so a render is a function of its data. The
  React Compiler lint enforces this.
- **Safe actions.** Cancel needs a second click to confirm. Every enqueue from the form carries a
  fresh `Idempotency-Key`, so a double submit returns the same job. Bulk requeue runs 4 requests
  at a time and reports failures per job. A job that is no longer dead returns 409 with the
  reason, which the page shows.

title: Job Scheduler design: 11. Scaling path and limitations
text:
**Where the bottleneck is.** PostgreSQL writes: a successful job costs one insert and two
updates of its `jobs` row (plus one more update if it was scheduled for later) and one insert
and one update of its `executions` row.
In the peak benchmark PostgreSQL sustained ≈1,500 jobs/s using about one CPU core, with the
API processes as the actual bottleneck (see BENCHMARKS.md). The API, workers and schedulers scale
horizontally.

**Next steps if 100×:**
1. Partition `jobs` by time (or by status: hot "active" table + "archive"), making retention a
   cheap `DROP PARTITION` instead of `DELETE`.
2. Batch claims (claim N ids in one statement) and batch completions to cut round trips.
3. Shard by queue across PostgreSQL clusters; one stream per queue already maps cleanly.
4. PgBouncer in transaction mode between many workers and PostgreSQL.
5. Redis Cluster: streams are per-queue keys, so they shard naturally.

**Deliberate limitations**
- No priorities within a queue (use separate queues and dedicate workers).
- No cron/recurring schedules or workflows (chains, fan-in).
- Sync handlers cannot be forcibly killed on timeout (a Python limitation; use async handlers or
  a process pool for hard isolation).
- `GET /v1/stats` does a `GROUP BY` over the tenant's jobs; at large scale this should read
  counters maintained incrementally.

title: Job Scheduler benchmarks: Where the bottleneck is (and isn't)
text:
- **API CPU.** Under peak load the API processes were the busiest containers: request parsing and
  validation, auth, the rate-limit script, an INSERT and an XADD per request. The API is stateless,
  so it scales horizontally.
- **Not PostgreSQL fsync.** With `synchronous_commit = off` (an experiment only; it is on in every
  reported run) throughput rose by only ~18%, so commit latency is not the limit at this scale.
  PostgreSQL CPU was about 1.1 of 8 cores.
- **Measurement pitfall found along the way.** A single load generator on the macOS host topped out
  near 500 requests/s because of Colima's host→VM port forwarding, while the containers were far
  from saturated. Moving the generators into the Docker network removed that artificial ceiling.
  Lesson: check where the time goes before blaming the system under test.

title: Job Scheduler benchmarks: Methodology notes
text:
- **Open-loop generation.** Request *i* is due at `t0 + i / rate` whether or not earlier
  requests have returned. A closed-loop generator (send, wait, send) slows down when the server
  slows down and under-reports tail latency ("coordinated omission"). Latency is reported both from
  the actual send time and from the intended send time.
- **Idempotent submission.** Each request carries `Idempotency-Key: -`, so a generator
  retry can never inflate the job count.
- **The audit is SQL.** Exactly-once is checked as `count(rows) = count(DISTINCT job_id)` on the
  ledger, joined against job status. It also checks succeeded jobs with no effect and effects for
  jobs that did not succeed.

title: Job Scheduler benchmarks: 3. Dashboard end to end (Playwright)
text:
`web/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts` against the compose stack (API, scheduler, 3 workers × 32
concurrency, `JOBQ_LEASE_S=10`), in headless Chromium. It signs in, enqueues N `examples.ledger`
jobs (3 s of work each), waits until one worker is running more than 5 of them, and SIGKILLs
that worker's container. Then it waits for every job to succeed and audits PostgreSQL. Last, it
opens a taken-over job in the dashboard: attempt 1 must show `lease expired` on the killed
worker, and the last attempt `succeeded`.

| Run | Jobs | Killed | Jobs taken over (attempts > 1) | Ledger rows / distinct jobs | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 200 | worker-2 | 32 | 200 / 200 | passed |
| 2 | 500 | worker-2 | 32 | 500 / 500 | passed |
| 3 | 500 | worker-2 | 32 | 500 / 500 | passed |
| 4 | 500 | worker-2 | 32 | 500 / 500 | passed |

32 is the killed worker's full concurrency: every job it was running was taken over once its
lease expired, and none was committed twice.

[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/CDC-Pipeline/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Log-based change data capture that keeps a PostgreSQL replica in sync with an operational MySQL
database (**inserts, updates and deletes**) in about a tenth of a second, and *proves* the replica
equals the source after crashes and live schema changes.

Debezium reads the MySQL binlog and publishes every row change to Kafka, keyed by primary key. A
Python sink (confluent-kafka + psycopg 3) applies the changes idempotently, keyed on primary key
and **binlog position**, and evolves the target schema on the fly.

```mermaid

    W[Workload8 writer processes] -->|orders, items, stock,customers, purges| M[(MySQL 8.4ROW binlog, GTID)]
    M -->|binlog| D[DebeziumKafka Connect]
```

| Deletes can't be undone by replays | soft deletes keep the position, so a replayed insert stays rejected |
| Schema changes without downtime | the Connect schema in every event → `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` in the same transaction, under an advisory lock |
| Fast failover | static group membership and cooperative-sticky rebalancing |
| Proof | catch-up barrier (marker row + zero consumer lag), then per-table row comparison and SHA-256 |

title: CDC Pipeline design: Goal
text:
Keep a PostgreSQL replica of an operational MySQL database continuously in sync, with
**inserts, updates and deletes**, within seconds, and be able to *prove* the replica equals the
source after crashes and schema changes.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Architecture
text:
```
MySQL 8.4 ──binlog (ROW, FULL images, GTID)──▶ Debezium MySQL connector (Kafka Connect)
                                                   │ one topic per table, 3 partitions,
                                                   │ message key = primary key
                                                   ▼
                                                 Kafka (KRaft)
                                                   │ consumer group, static membership,
                                                   │ cooperative-sticky rebalancing
                                                   ▼
                                     cdcpipe sink × N (Python, confluent-kafka)
                                                   │ batch → dedupe → COPY + guarded MERGE
                                                   ▼
                                     PostgreSQL 16 (replica schema + _cdc.consumer_stats)
```

Why log-based CDC and not polling `updated_at` (which Project 1 does):

| | Polling `updated_at` | Binlog CDC |
|---|---|---|
| Deletes | invisible | captured (with the full before-image) |
| Intermediate states | lost if a row changes twice between polls | every change, in commit order |
| Late commits | needs a lookback window | none: the binlog is in commit order |
| Load on the source | a query per table per poll | reads the log the server writes anyway |
| Latency | the poll interval | ~100 ms here |
| Cost | trivial | Kafka + Connect to operate |

title: CDC Pipeline design: What the probe showed
text:
Before writing the sink I registered a connector and inspected real events from a transaction
that updated one row twice and inserted two rows in one statement:

| Event | `source.pos` | `source.row` |
|---|---|---|
| update #1, row 1 | 990 | 0 |
| update #2, row 1 (same transaction) | 1134 | 0 |
| multi-row insert, row 2 | 1278 | 0 |
| multi-row insert, row 3 | 1278 | 1 |

So **(binlog file number, pos, row) is strictly increasing**, even inside one transaction, and
works as a per-row version. `source.ts_us` is the MySQL commit time in microseconds, which is
what the lag measurement uses.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Idempotent apply
text:
Every target row stores the position of the event that produced it (`_src_file`, `_src_pos`,
`_src_row`). A batch is applied as

```sql
INSERT INTO shop.t AS t (...) SELECT ... FROM _stage
ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET ... 
WHERE (t._src_file, t._src_pos, t._src_row) < (EXCLUDED._src_file, EXCLUDED._src_pos, EXCLUDED._src_row)
```

The consequences:
- **Replays are no-ops.** After a crash, a rebalance or a Debezium restart, an event that was
  already applied has an equal position and is skipped.
- **Order doesn't matter.** An older event arriving after a newer one can't overwrite it.
- Within a batch, only the newest event per key is staged (fewer writes, and one key per
  `ON CONFLICT` statement, which PostgreSQL requires).

title: CDC Pipeline design: Delivery: at-least-once plus idempotence
text:
```
consume batch → PostgreSQL BEGIN … MERGE … COMMIT → Kafka commit offsets
```

| Crash point | What happens on restart |
|---|---|
| before the PostgreSQL commit | transaction rolled back; the batch is re-consumed and applied |
| between the PostgreSQL and Kafka commits | the batch is re-consumed; every event is stale, so nothing changes |
| after the Kafka commit | nothing to redo |

Tests kill a sink at each of the first two points (`CDCPIPE_HANG` freezes it there, then SIGKILL)
and check the replica is identical to the source afterwards.

The alternative is exactly-once by storing Kafka offsets in PostgreSQL in the same transaction,
and seeking to them on startup. It's equivalent in effect here, but idempotent apply also
protects against duplicates from *upstream* (Debezium re-emits events after its own restarts),
which offset-in-target alone wouldn't.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Deletes are soft
text:
A delete event is applied as an upsert of its before-image with `_deleted = true` and the
delete's position. A hard `DELETE` would discard the position, and a replayed older insert would
then resurrect the row. A test does exactly that replay. Views or a periodic purge can hide or
remove soft-deleted rows; the verifier compares only live rows.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Schema evolution without downtime
text:
Every message carries its Kafka Connect schema. The sink compares it with the target table
(cached, re-read from `pg_catalog` under a per-table advisory lock when something differs):

| Source change | Sink action |
|---|---|
| new column | `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` (nullable), in the same transaction as the batch that first carries it |
| wider DECIMAL | `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` to the new precision |
| incompatible type change | stop with `SchemaConflict`; never guess |
| dropped column | the column stays and is NULL from then on (full row images) |

Because MySQL sends full row images, the merge writes *every* target column. A column the event
doesn't carry is set to NULL. An early version only updated the event's own columns and left a
stale value behind when a table was recreated without that column. Leftover test data exposed it.

In the 1M-event run, `ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN loyalty_tier` ran at event 500,000 while
8 writers and 3 sinks kept going. MySQL 8 does it `ALGORITHM=INSTANT`, Debezium picks the DDL up
from the binlog, and the sink adds the column on the first event that has it.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Scaling and rebalancing
text:
- Debezium keys every message by primary key, so all changes to one row go to one partition, in
  order. Three partitions per table allow three sinks in parallel.
- **Static membership** (`group.instance.id`): a sink that restarts with the same id gets its
  partitions back immediately instead of waiting out the session timeout.
- **Cooperative-sticky** assignment: when a new table's topic appears, only the new partitions
  move. With the default eager assignor every sink stopped while partitions were reshuffled.
- Bootstrap DDL (schema and stats table) runs under an advisory lock. Three sinks starting
  together once raced on `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS`, which isn't atomic in PostgreSQL.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Latency tuning
text:
| Setting | Default | Here | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Debezium `poll.interval.ms` | 500 | 50 | Debezium waits this long between batches when idle |
| librdkafka `fetch.wait.max.ms` | 500 | 20 | the broker holds a fetch this long waiting for data |
| `topic.metadata.refresh.interval.ms` | 300000 | 1000 | a regex subscription only sees new topics on refresh |
| producer `linger.ms` | 0 | 5 | small batching, compressed with lz4 |

Before the metadata change, the first events of every table created during the run waited for
the next refresh: p99 was 4.5 s even with no failures.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Verification
text:
`cdcpipe verify`:

1. **Catch-up barrier.** Insert a marker row into MySQL, wait until it's applied, then wait until
   the consumer group has zero lag on every partition. Debezium emits in binlog order, so
   everything before the marker has been produced.
2. **Row-by-row comparison** under a consistent MySQL snapshot. Values are normalized to one text
   form on both sides (exact decimals, microsecond timestamps, a NULL sentinel). Reported per
   table: missing, extra and mismatched rows, plus a **SHA-256 checksum** over the sorted rows.

The benchmark fails if any table differs.

title: CDC Pipeline design: Known limits
text:
- One MySQL source, so positions compare within one binlog sequence. With failover to a replica,
  positions change servers; GTID-based ordering would be needed.
- `TRUNCATE` events aren't supported (the sink stops on them).
- Soft-deleted rows accumulate; production would purge them after a retention period.
- The replica is eventually consistent *per row*, not per transaction: a reader can see an order
  before its items land, because they're on different partitions. Debezium's transaction
  metadata topic could be used to apply whole transactions atomically.
