title: CDC Pipeline results: Bugs found while building it
text:
1. **Sinks crashed on startup** with "unknown topic" when they subscribed before Debezium had
   created the topics. A calibration run still passed with one surviving sink doing everything.
   It was only noticed because the scheduled kill hit an already-dead process. Fix: treat it as
   transient. The benchmark now fails if any sink exits unexpectedly.
2. **Race on bootstrap DDL**: three sinks starting together collided on `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT
   EXISTS`, which isn't atomic in PostgreSQL. Fix: an advisory lock.
3. **Stale column values**: the merge only wrote the event's own columns. Leftover data from an
   earlier run (a recreated table without the new column) exposed it. With full row images the
   merge must write every target column.
4. **Type changes went unnoticed**: the schema check compared column *names* only, so a widened
   DECIMAL failed at insert. Found by a unit test; the check now compares types and widens.
5. **A sink died on a rejected offset commit** (found by CI). When the killed sink rejoined, the
   group generation changed between another sink's PostgreSQL commit and its Kafka offset commit,
   and the commit failed with `ILLEGAL_GENERATION`. The sink treated it as fatal. It's harmless by
   design: the batch is already applied, and the partition's new owner replays it as no-ops. Fix:
   tolerate rebalance-related commit errors (counted and logged), and keep everything else fatal.

title: Event Streaming overview: livefeed: real-time event streaming
text:
[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Real-Time-Event-Streaming/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A live event feed, demoed as a real-time cricket scoreboard with a React web app. Producers
publish events, PostgreSQL stores them in order, and every WebSocket subscriber on any instance
(a browser tab or the Python SDK) receives each event **exactly once, in order**. That holds
through reconnects, instance crashes, Redis failures and slow clients.

**Backend:** Python 3.12, asyncio, FastAPI + WebSockets, PostgreSQL (ordered log and snapshots),
Redis pub/sub (cross-instance fan-out), nginx, Docker, GitHub Actions.
**Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, React Router; tested with
Vitest, Testing Library and Playwright.

title: Event Streaming overview: How it works
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[Producers] -->|POST events + event_id| LB[nginx]
    C[1,000 WebSocket clients] |cursor resume| LB
    LB --> I1[instance 1] & I2[instance 2] & I3[instance 3]
    I1 & I2 & I3 -->|append under per-stream row lockreplay, gap fill, snapshots| PG[(PostgreSQLstreams, events)]
    I1 & I2 & I3 |PUBLISH / SUBSCRIBEbest effort| R[(Redis pub/sub)]
```

title: Event Streaming overview: How it works
text:
- **Ordering.** Appends lock the stream's row, so `seq = last_seq + 1` is assigned in commit
  order. If seq N is visible, everything before it is too.
- **Fan-out.** After commit the event is published to Redis. Each instance forwards it to its
  local clients. The event is serialised once and the same bytes go to every client.
- **Pub/sub is allowed to fail.** Each instance tracks the last seq it delivered per stream. It
  drops duplicates and fills gaps from PostgreSQL. A 1-second resync loop catches lost final
  messages. Out-of-order delivery across instances is repaired the same way.
- **Race-free resume.** A reconnecting client is registered *before* its history replay, and
  live events are buffered meanwhile. Replay is paged, flow-controlled and **bounded**: a cursor
  more than 10,000 behind gets a snapshot instead.
- **Backpressure.** Each client has a bounded queue and its own writer task. A client that falls
  behind is closed with `4008` and resumes from its cursor. Memory stays bounded and other clients
  are never slowed. Producers get `429` (token bucket) or `503` (load shedding).
- **One recovery path.** Network drops, crashes, deploys (`1012`), slow consumers (`4008`) and
  detected gaps (`4009`) all end the same way: reconnect and resume from the cursor.

Full reasoning, alternatives and failure analysis: **docs/DESIGN.md**.

title: Event Streaming overview: Web app
text:
`web/` is a React + TypeScript app that every instance serves at `/` (the Docker image builds it).

- **Matches** (`/`): live and finished matches with their scores, refreshed every 2 seconds.
- **Match** (`/m/`): scoreboard, ball by ball feed and a connection panel that makes the
  guarantees visible: cursor, events applied, duplicates dropped, gaps resynced, reconnects,
  lag behind the server, ping, and why the last connection closed. **Simulate network drop**
  kills the socket so you can watch it resume.

The browser speaks the same protocol as the Python SDK through its own client,
`web/src/feed/client.ts`. It keeps a cursor and accepts only seq =
cursor + 1, so it drops duplicates and treats any gap as a reason to reconnect from its cursor.
It reconnects straight away after a restart (`1012`) or a resync, and backs off exponentially with
jitter after network failures. A heartbeat watchdog detects dead connections, and it waits for the
browser's `online` event instead of retrying while offline. Joining mid-match gives a snapshot,
and the last 30 balls are fetched over REST to fill the feed. The TypeScript reducer must match the
Python one exactly. `tests/test_web_contract.py` writes the Python states for three simulated
matches, and `reducers.test.ts` replays them event by event.

title: Event Streaming design: livefeed: Design
text:
A service that takes ordered events from producers (e.g. a live match: scores, wickets,
commentary) and pushes them to many WebSocket subscribers across several server instances. Each
section states the problem, the decision, and the alternatives.

title: Event Streaming design: 1. Requirements
text:
**Functional**
- Producers append events to a stream; each gets a per-stream sequence number (`seq`).
- Subscribers get live events over WebSocket; a new subscriber gets a **snapshot** of the
  current state plus everything after it.
- A reconnecting subscriber resumes from its **cursor** (last seq it processed).
- History over HTTP; per-stream materialised state.

**Guarantees**
- **Per-stream total order**: every subscriber sees seq 1, 2, 3, … with no gaps, duplicates or
  reordering, including across reconnects, instance crashes and Redis failures.
- **Durability**: an acknowledged publish is committed and will reach every subscriber.
- **Isolation**: a slow or stuck client cannot slow others down or exhaust server memory.
- **Scale-out**: any number of stateless instances behind a load balancer.

**Targets**: 1,000 concurrent clients across 3 instances, 100,000 events, p95 live delivery
:"` to `lf:s:`. Each instance keeps
**one** pub/sub connection, subscribed only to streams that have local clients (reference-counted
channels, unsubscribed after a linger period).

The event is serialised **once** (orjson) and the same bytes are forwarded to every subscriber
on every instance. WebSocket frames are built by concatenating pre-serialised events.

title: Event Streaming design: Why Redis pub/sub is allowed to be unreliable
text:
Pub/sub is fire-and-forget: a subscriber that is reconnecting misses messages, and messages from
*different publishers* (instances) can arrive out of order. For example, instance A commits seq 5
and instance B commits seq 6, but B's PUBLISH lands first. Instead of fighting that, each
instance treats pub/sub as a hint and repairs it:

**Per-stream channel pump** (one task per stream per instance, processing its inbox in order):

| Message seq vs channel `last_seq` | Action |
|---|---|
| `seq  last_seq + 1` | **gap** → read `(last_seq, seq)` from PostgreSQL, deliver, then this one |

The gap fill always succeeds because of the ordering property in §3. A **resync loop** (every 1 s)
compares each active channel with `streams.last_seq` in one query. That catches a lost *final*
message, which no later message would reveal. After a pub/sub reconnect, every channel is
resynced immediately. If the channel's inbox overflows, messages are dropped on purpose and the
next seq reveals the gap.

**Why not Redis Streams or Kafka for fan-out?** Either would give a replayable buffer, but
PostgreSQL already is the replayable log (primary-key range scans on `(stream_id, seq)`). A
second durable log would be a second source of truth to keep consistent. Pub/sub gives the
lowest latency for the broadcast and costs nothing when it fails.

title: Event Streaming design: 5. Joining and resuming without a race
text:
The classic bug: a client asks for history, then subscribes to live events, and anything
published between the two is lost (or, done in the other order, duplicated). livefeed avoids it:

1. **Register first**: the session joins the channel in *buffering* mode. Live events for it are
   buffered, not sent.
2. **Catch up**: no cursor → send snapshot `(state, seq)`. With a cursor → replay `seq > cursor`
   from PostgreSQL in pages of 500, flow-controlled by the session's queue. If the cursor is more
   than `max_replay` (10,000) behind, or ahead of the stream, send a snapshot with a `reason`
   instead: **bounded replay**.
3. **Go live**: flush the buffer, skipping anything the replay already covered, then deliver
   directly.

The replay starts *after* registration, so replay + buffer covers every seq. If a session ever
sees a gap anyway, it is closed with **4009** and the client reconnects with its cursor. The whole
system has **one recovery path**: disconnect and resume from the cursor. The same path handles
network drops, instance crashes, slow consumers and deploys.

When an instance creates a channel, it subscribes to Redis *before* reading `last_seq` from
PostgreSQL, so nothing committed after the read can be missed.

title: Event Streaming design: 6. Backpressure and slow consumers
text:
- The channel pump **never blocks on a client**: `Session.deliver()` is synchronous and uses
  `put_nowait` on a bounded queue (default 2,000 events).
- Each session has its own **writer task** that batches consecutive events (up to 200) into one
  frame and awaits the socket. The ASGI server's transport flow control makes that await block
  when the kernel buffer is full, so a stuck client stops draining its queue.
- When the queue is full, the client is **closed with 4008**. It loses nothing: it reconnects and
  resumes from its cursor via replay, which is itself flow-controlled. The server spends
  O(queue size) memory per client, never unbounded. Fast clients are unaffected (tested: a client
  that stops reading is cut off after ~1 MB while another client receives all 2,000 events without
  a single reconnect).
- The pump yields to the event loop after every message, so writers drain in between. Without
  that, a burst would fill every queue before any writer ran.
- **Producer side**: per-key token bucket (429) and a per-instance cap on in-flight publishes
  (503 + `Retry-After`). Past capacity the instance sheds load immediately instead of queueing
  until everyone times out.

Alternatives: dropping events for slow clients (breaks the ordering guarantee), or buffering
without bound (one slow phone can take down the server). Disconnect-and-resume keeps both
guarantees.

title: Event Streaming design: 7. Liveness: heartbeats
text:
- WebSocket protocol pings (uvicorn, every 20 s, 20 s timeout) detect dead TCP peers that never
  sent a FIN (e.g. a phone that lost signal).
- An application-level heartbeat every 15 s carries `seq` (last sent to you) and `head` (latest
  known). A client can detect staleness even through proxies that answer pings themselves.
- Clients may send `{"type":"ping"}` and get a pong.

title: Event Streaming design: 8. Failure modes
text:
| Failure | Effect | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Client network drop | TCP dies (1006) | SDK reconnects with jittered backoff, resumes from cursor |
| Instance SIGKILL | Its clients drop; nginx routes new connections elsewhere | Clients resume from their cursors on other instances; no state is lost (instances are stateless) |
| Instance deploy / SIGTERM | Clients get **1012** | Immediate resume elsewhere |
| Redis pub/sub connection killed | Messages missed | Subscriber reconnects, resubscribes, resyncs all channels from PostgreSQL |
| Redis down | Publishes still commit (PUBLISH failure is logged); rate limiter fails open | Resync loop delivers from PostgreSQL within ~1 s |
| Out-of-order pub/sub delivery | Gap then duplicate | Gap fill from PostgreSQL, duplicate dropped |
| Slow / stuck client | Queue fills | **4008**, resume from cursor |
| Very old cursor | Replay would be huge | Snapshot with `reason: cursor_expired` |
| Producer retry after timeout | Might double-publish | `event_id` dedupe returns the original seq |
| PostgreSQL down | Publishes fail (5xx); live fan-out of already-committed events continues | Producers retry with the same event ids |

title: Event Streaming design: 9. Scaling path
text:
- **Instances**: stateless; add more behind the balancer. Each instance subscribes only to the
  streams its clients watch.
- **Hot stream** (one match, 1M viewers): fan-out work is per instance, not per stream, so spread
  its viewers across instances. Past that, add a tier of edge relays that subscribe once
  upstream.
- **Many streams**: pub/sub channels are cheap; Redis Cluster shards pub/sub (sharded pub/sub in
  Redis 7, `SPUBLISH`).
- **PostgreSQL**: appends are per-stream serial and parallel across streams. Partition `events`
  by time for retention; archive old streams. Replays are primary-key range scans.

title: Event Streaming design: 10. The browser client
text:
The web app (`web/`) does not trust the server blindly; it checks the same invariant the server
promises. `FeedClient` keeps a cursor and folds an item only if `seq == cursor + 1`. Anything at or
below the cursor is a duplicate and is dropped. Anything above it is a gap: the client abandons
the socket (close `4000`) and reconnects from its cursor instead of applying past a hole.

title: Event Streaming design: 10. The browser client
text:
- **One recovery path, again.** A network drop, an instance restart (`1012`), a slow-consumer
  cut-off (`4008`), a server resync (`4009`), a client-side gap and a heartbeat timeout all end in
  a reconnect with `?cursor=N`. Server-initiated ones reconnect at once, with up to 250 ms of
  jitter so a restarted instance's clients do not all reconnect at once. Network failures back
  off exponentially with full jitter (0.5 s doubling up to 10 s), and the backoff resets after 5
  stable seconds.
- **Abandoned sockets are fenced.** Each socket gets a generation number. Once the client gives
  up on a socket, anything it still delivers is ignored. Without that, a late frame from the old
  socket could be applied after the new socket's replay.
- **Liveness.** Any frame re-arms a 40-second watchdog (the server heartbeats every 15 s). An
  application ping every 10 s measures round-trip time. While the browser reports offline, the
  client waits for the `online` event instead of retrying.
- **State.** The page starts from the server's snapshot and folds later events with a TypeScript
  port of the reducer. A contract test keeps the two identical: Python writes the state after
  every event of three simulated matches, and the TypeScript reducer must reproduce each one.
- **React.** The client is a plain class with `subscribe` / `getSnapshot`, and the page reads it
  with `useSyncExternalStore`. Each update creates a new immutable snapshot, so components
  re-render only when something changed and never see a torn state. REST data (the match list
  and the mid-match backfill) uses TanStack Query.

title: Event Streaming design: 11. Limitations (deliberate)
text:
- One stream per WebSocket connection (multiplexing many streams is a straightforward extension).
- Subscribers are unauthenticated (public live feeds). Private streams would need signed,
  expiring subscribe tokens.
- No event retention job yet; bounded replay plus snapshots already make old events unnecessary
  for clients.

|---|---|
| Clients that ended with every event | **1,000 / 1,000** |
| Deliveries / expected | **5,000,000 / 5,000,000** |
| Duplicate seqs received (protocol level, before SDK dedupe) | **0** |

title: Event Streaming benchmarks: 1. 1,000 clients, 100,000 events, continuous chaos
text:

violation *before* it would drop or repair anything, so its own safety net cannot hide a server
bug. Every client's final cursor was also compared with `streams.last_seq` in PostgreSQL.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads overview: Streaming Consumer Benchmark: asyncio vs virtual threads
text:
[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Streaming-Consumer-Benchmark/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

The fan-out hot path from my real-time streaming platform,
Kafka in and thousands of TCP sockets out, **written twice**:

- **Java 21**: one virtual thread per connection, plain blocking I/O, no event loop.
- **Python 3.12**: asyncio on uvloop, one event loop per process.

Both implement the same protocol (checked by a shared conformance suite against real Kafka) and are
driven by **one load harness**: an open-loop Kafka producer and a client swarm that audits every
sequence number and measures end-to-end latency. Every run is a cold container with the warm-up
window discarded; results are medians of repetitions.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads overview: Findings (details in docs/RESULTS.md)
text:
| 2 CPUs / 1 GiB per server | Java 21, virtual threads | Python, asyncio |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 5,000 connections (≤ 50k deliveries/s) | p50 ≈ 2 ms, p99 ≈ 4-5 ms | p50 ≈ 2 ms, p99 ≈ 5-10 ms |
| 10,000 connections (100k deliveries/s) | p99 **8 ms** | 1 process: p99 **253 ms** (one core at 100%) · 2 processes: 18 ms |
| 20,000 connections (200k deliveries/s) | 2 dispatch threads: p50 **2.5 ms**, p99 67 ms | 2 processes: p50 184 ms |
| 320,000 deliveries/s (2,000 connections) | p99 25-28 ms | 1 process: 57 ms · 2 processes: 161 ms |
| memory per connection | ≈ 28 KiB (+190 MiB JVM base) | ≈ 12 KiB (+45 MiB base) |
| JVM warm-up | p99 14 ms in the first second only, then ≈ 3 ms | none |
| slow consumers | fast clients unaffected; stalled ones cut off and resumed, 0 lost | same; asyncio's larger user-space buffer rides out ~2× more of each stall |
| correctness (every run) | 0 duplicates, 0 gaps | 0 duplicates, 0 gaps |

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads overview: Findings (details in docs/RESULTS.md)
text:
What the measurements uncovered along the way:
- **Java ran out of memory at 10k connections** in its first version: 64 KiB write buffers plus
  an 8 KiB reader per connection. Right-sizing them cut memory at 5k connections from 880 to
  337 MiB.
- **One dispatch thread concentrated virtual-thread wake-ups on one carrier.** At 20k
  connections, one carrier ran at 81% while the other sat idle. GC and carrier count were ruled out
  with GC logs and what-if runs. Two dispatch threads took p50 from 87 ms to 2.3 ms.
- **Linux silently absorbed stalled clients** in up to 4 MiB of kernel send buffer per socket.
  Capping `SO_SNDBUF` made backpressure reach the application's bounded queue.

**Read next:** docs/RESULTS.md (charts and findings) ·
docs/DESIGN.md (how both servers work, fairness controls).

text:
```bash

make conformance   # identical behaviour from all four, against real Kafka
make smoke         # ~1 minute benchmark
make bench         # every experiment in RESULTS.md (~3 hours)

```

The protocol is newline-delimited TCP: `SUB  ` → `{"type":"ok","head":H,"reset":false}`
followed by events in `seq` order. See DESIGN.md §2.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 1. The question
text:
My streaming platform (Real-Time-Event-Streaming)
fans events out to thousands of sockets from a Python asyncio event loop. Java 21 made a
different model practical: **one cheap virtual thread per connection, with plain blocking code**.
This project reimplements the fan-out hot path in both models and measures them under one harness:

- How do latency, throughput, CPU and memory behave as connections and event rates grow?
- Where do the two models *diverge*, especially with slow consumers and backpressure?

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 2. What both servers do (identical contract)
text:
```
Kafka topic "events" (12 partitions, key = stream)
        │  one consumer, all partitions, starting at the end
        ▼
  parse {stream, seq} ──► per-stream state: ring buffer (last 10,000) + subscribers
        │                  publish = append + non-blocking offer to every subscriber queue
        ▼
  per-connection bounded queue (1,000 events) ──► writer ──► TCP socket
```

**Protocol** (newline-delimited, identical for both; checked by `harness/tests/test_conformance.py`):

| Client sends | Server replies |
|---|---|
| `SUB  -1` | `{"type":"ok","head":H,"reset":false}` then every new event |
| `SUB  ` | `ok`, then every event after `cursor` from the ring buffer, then live |
| cursor older than the buffer / ahead of the stream | `{"type":"ok","head":H,"reset":true}` (client resumes at H) |
| `STATS` | one JSON line of counters |
| anything else | `{"type":"error",...}` |

Events are the Kafka record bytes plus `\n`, built once and shared by every connection.

**Why plain TCP, not WebSockets?** The goal is to compare concurrency models, not WebSocket
libraries. The JDK has no WebSocket server, and a framework (Jetty, Netty) would bring its own
threading model into the measurement.

**Why Kafka?** It is the realistic source for a fan-out tier. Keying by stream keeps each stream
ordered on one partition. Both servers use the same consumer settings (`fetch.max.wait.ms=5`,
`max.poll.records=5000`, assign all partitions, seek to end).

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: Java 21: virtual thread per connection (`java-server/`)
text:
- `ServerSocket.accept()` → `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`: one virtual thread
  per client, running a straight-line blocking loop: `queue.take()` → `write` → `flush`.
- **Backpressure is a blocking `write()`**. When a client stops reading, the kernel buffer fills,
  `write` blocks, and only that virtual thread parks. Its carrier (OS) thread moves on to other
  connections.
- A **platform** thread runs the Kafka poll loop (`KafkaConsumer` is not thread-safe) and calls
  `StreamState.publish`, which offers to each subscriber's `ArrayBlockingQueue` without blocking.
  With `FANOUT_CONSUMERS=2` there are two such threads, each owning half the partitions (a stream
  lives on one partition, so order is kept). This matters more than it looks: on JDK 21, virtual
  threads woken from a single platform thread piled up on one carrier (see RESULTS.md §4), so
  it is benchmarked as a separate implementation (`java-2disp`).
- Stream state is guarded by a `ReentrantLock`, not `synchronized`: on Java 21 a virtual thread
  blocking inside `synchronized` pins its carrier (fixed in JDK 24 by JEP 491).
- Detecting a departed client: the writer spends its life parked in `take()`, so a second virtual
  thread per connection blocks on `read()` and interrupts the writer at EOF. Two threads per
  connection is fine when threads cost a few hundred bytes of stack.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: Python: asyncio event loop (`python-server/`)
text:
- `asyncio.start_server` on **uvloop**: one thread, one event loop, a coroutine per connection.
- **Backpressure is `await writer.drain()`**, which suspends the writer coroutine while the
  transport's buffer is above its high-water mark.
- The Kafka loop (`aiokafka`) and all connections share the same thread, so `publish` and
  `attach` can never interleave. No locks are needed.
- Departed clients: a small reader task awaits EOF and wakes the writer.
- **Multi-core**: one loop uses one core. The standard answer is N independent processes sharing
  the port (`SO_REUSEPORT`, `FANOUT_WORKERS=2`): the kernel spreads connections, and each
  process consumes Kafka and serves its own clients. It is benchmarked as a third
  implementation (`python-2proc`).

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: Shared semantics
text:
- **Kernel buffers**: both servers can cap each socket's send buffer (`FANOUT_SNDBUF`). Linux
  otherwise auto-grows it up to 4 MiB per connection, which quietly absorbs a stalled client's
  backlog. At 10k connections that is up to 40 GiB of kernel memory the server doesn't account for.
- **Ordering**: per-stream `seq` from the producer; the server drops `seq <= head` (Kafka
  redelivery). Clients audit contiguity.
- **Race-free join**: registering a subscriber and snapshotting its replay happen atomically
  (the lock in Java, a single non-awaiting code path in Python).
- **Slow consumers**: `offer` fails when the queue is full → the connection is closed → the client
  reconnects with its cursor and replays from the ring buffer (or resets if too far behind).
  Fast clients never wait for slow ones.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 4. The harness (one for both)
text:
`harness/src/bench/`:
- `producer.py`: open-loop Kafka producer (`rate` events/s round-robin over `streams`), stamping
  `sent_at` and per-stream `seq`.
- `clients.py`: N TCP subscribers over 6 processes (uvloop `Protocol`s, no buffering library).
  It records latency (receive − `sent_at`) into mergeable log histograms (2% precision), audits
  duplicates and gaps, reconnects with the cursor when cut off, and optionally stalls a fraction of
  clients by pausing the socket read (true TCP-level slowness). A parallel Kafka-only consumer
  measures the broker's share of the latency.
- `run.py`: for every run it stops the other servers, **recreates the server container** (cold
  start), connects clients, produces for `warmup + measure + 5` s, **discards the warm-up window**,
  samples server and harness CPU/memory with `docker stats`, then checks every client reached the
  producer's final seq.

**Implementations measured**: `java` (1 dispatch thread), `java-2disp` (2 dispatch threads),
`python` (1 event loop), `python-2proc` (2 processes). Each language gets a "default" and a
"use both cores" configuration.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 4. The harness (one for both)
text:
**Fairness controls**
- Same container limits for every server: 2 CPUs, 1 GiB. Clients get 6 CPUs, the producer 1,
  Kafka 2, on a 12-vCPU VM.
- Same workload files, seeds, Kafka topic, consumer settings and queue/ring sizes.
- Harness CPU is recorded for every run; a run where the harness nears its limit would measure the
  harness, not the server.
- JVM warm-up: 30 s discarded per run, plus a dedicated cold-start experiment (per-second p99) that
  shows how long warm-up actually takes; JMH with warm-up iterations and forks for the hot path.
- Repetitions: medians of 3 for scaling (min-max bands on the charts).

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 5. Where the models diverge (summary; numbers in RESULTS.md)
text:
| Concern | Java virtual threads | Python asyncio |
|---|---|---|
| Programming model | Blocking, straight-line; stack traces make sense | `async`/`await` everywhere; one blocking call stalls every client |
| Cores | All cores from one process | One core per process; scale with processes (`SO_REUSEPORT`) |
| Per-connection memory | Thread stack + buffers; must be sized deliberately | Small: a coroutine, a deque, transport buffers |
| Slow client | Its writer thread parks in `write()`; queue fills; cut off | `drain()` suspends its coroutine; queue fills; cut off |
| Detecting disconnects | Needs a reader (second virtual thread) | Transport callbacks / a reader task |
| Shared state | Needs locks (and care with pinning on Java 21) | No locks (single thread) |
| Dispatch parallelism | Threads you choose; one dispatcher concentrated wake-ups on one carrier | One loop per process; parallel only across processes |
| Warm-up | JIT: slower first second | None |

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads design: 6. Limitations
text:
- One machine: clients, producer, Kafka and the server share a laptop (in separate containers with
  CPU limits). Absolute numbers are laptop numbers; the comparison is the point.
- One Kafka broker, no replication (the broker is not what is being measured; the Kafka-only
  probe shows its share).
- Python's second process doubles Kafka consumption (each process consumes every event), which a
  production design might avoid with partition-aware routing.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: Results
text:
Four implementations under one harness: **Java 21 virtual threads** with 1 or 2 Kafka dispatch
threads, and **Python asyncio** with 1 or 2 processes. Every server runs in a container limited
to **2 CPUs and 1 GiB**. The clients get 6 CPUs, the producer 1 and Kafka 2, on a 12-vCPU Colima VM
(MacBook Pro, Apple M5 Pro). Every run starts a fresh server container and discards the first 30 s.
Scaling points are the **median of 3 runs** (shaded bands on the charts show min to max).
Latency is end to end: producer send → Kafka → server → client receive.

Raw data: `results/`. All tables: `tables.md` (generated).
Correctness: **every run in every suite ended with 0 duplicate and 0 missing sequence numbers**,
and every client received the producer's final event.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 1. Scaling connections (1,000 events/s, 100 streams, so 10 deliveries/s per connection)
asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 1. Scaling connections (1,000 events/s, 100 streams, so 10 deliveries/s per connection)
text:
- Up to 5,000 connections all four are equivalent: about 2 ms median, which is mostly Kafka.
  The Kafka-only probe alone measures about 2 ms.
- **One asyncio event loop runs out at about 100k socket writes/s.** At 10k connections it sits at
  100% of one core and latency jumps from about 2 ms to 145 ms. That isn't a bug; it's the model:
  one thread. Two processes behind `SO_REUSEPORT` fix it at 10k (p99 18 ms) and use both cores
  (206% at 20k).
- **Java with a single dispatch thread fell over at 20k** with CPU to spare (114% of 200%). §4
  explains why; with two dispatch threads the p50 stays at 2.5 ms at 200k deliveries/s.

**Memory per connection** (slope between 5k and 20k connections): Java about 28 KiB, Python about
12 KiB. Java also starts at about 190 MiB of JVM and heap, versus about 45 MiB for Python.
Container memory includes heap the JVM has grown but not yet collected, so Java's figure is an
upper bound.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 1. Scaling connections (1,000 events/s, 100 streams, so 10 deliveries/s per connection)
text:
> **Finding: the first Java version ran out of memory at 10k connections.** It used 880 MiB at 5k
> connections because each connection eagerly allocated a 64 KiB `BufferedOutputStream` and an
> `InputStreamReader` (8 KiB decode buffer). An 8 KiB write buffer, which larger batches bypass,
> plus reading the command straight from the `InputStream`, brought 5k connections down to
> 337 MiB and made 10k and 20k possible. The threads were cheap; the buffers attached to them were
> not.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 2. Saturation (2,000 connections; raising the event rate)
text:
| offered deliveries/s | Java, 1 disp. | Java, 2 disp. | Python, 1 proc. | Python, 2 proc. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 80,000 | 6.1 ms | 7.3 | 16.5 | 8.6 |
| 160,000 | 11.8 | 12.0 | 45.2 (CPU 102%) | 18.2 |
| 320,000 | 24.9 | 28.1 | 57.3 (CPU 101%) | 160.5 (CPU 198%) |

*(p99)*

Everyone delivered 100% of events. With 2,000 connections, each connection receives more events
per wake-up, so writes batch well (up to 200 events per `write`), which is why single-process
Python still keeps up at 320k/s here while it could not at 10k connections × 10/s. **Cost follows
the number of socket writes and wake-ups, not the number of events.** Java's p99 grows slowly and
stays under 30 ms at 320k deliveries/s. Two Python processes reach 198% CPU and their tail rises
sharply at the top point.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 3. JVM warm-up
text:
| | p99, first second | seconds 1-5 | seconds 5-30 | after 30 s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Java (1 dispatcher) | **14.1 ms** | 3.2 | 4.3 | 3.8 |
| Java (2 dispatchers) | **17.8** | 3.4 | 4.0 | 4.2 |
| Python (1 process) | 5.1 | 4.8 | 3.6 | 4.5 |
| Python (2 processes) | 3.2 | 3.7 | 4.5 | 4.4 |

At 50k deliveries/s the JIT compiles the hot path within about a second: only the first second
shows a Java penalty. The 30 s discarded in every other run is therefore conservative. JMH
isolates the hot path with 5 warm-up iterations and 2 forks:

| hot-path operation | Java (JMH, warmed) | Python (timeit, best of 5) |
|---|---|---|
| parse one event (`stream`, `seq`) | 77-92 ns | 177 ns |
| publish to 10 subscribers | 48 ns | 766 ns |
| publish to 100 subscribers | 833 ns | 5,675 ns |
| publish to 1,000 subscribers | 10.7 µs | 54.9 µs |

Java's per-subscriber offer is about 5-7× cheaper in isolation. The end-to-end difference is much
smaller because both servers mostly wait on sockets and Kafka, which is why the macro benchmark,
not the micro one, decides.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 4. Diagnosing Java at 20,000 connections
text:
At 20k connections the single-dispatcher Java server had p50 = 87 ms while using only 114% of its
2 CPUs. What I tested (`results/whatif/`):

| what-if (20k connections, 200k deliveries/s) | p50 | p99 | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline: 1 GiB, 1 dispatch thread, 2 carriers | 88.6 ms | 192 ms | 114% |
| GC logging on: 71 pauses, **0.39 s total** in the run, max 19 ms, no full GC | 86.9 | 181 | 115% |
| 2 GiB memory limit | 56.2 | 157 | 123% |
| 4 carrier threads (`jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=4`) | 97.8 | 204 | 115% |
| per-thread CPU (`top -H`): **one carrier ~81%, the other ~8%**, Kafka thread ~7% | | | |
| **2 dispatch threads** (partitions split): carriers ~52% / ~52% | **2.3** | **62** | 161% |

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 4. Diagnosing Java at 20,000 connections
text:
- **Not GC**: pauses totalled 0.4 s over the run, and doubling memory helped only a little.
- **Not the carrier count**: with 4 carriers, one still did all the work.
- **The cause was the single dispatcher.** Every writer's virtual thread was unparked by one
  platform thread (the Kafka poll loop), and those continuations kept landing on one carrier.
  Splitting dispatch over two threads, each owning half the Kafka partitions (so per-stream order
  holds), balanced the carriers and brought p50 back to 2.3 ms.

Virtual threads remove the cost of threads, not scheduling effects. Measure per thread, not per
process.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 5. Slow consumers and backpressure (1,000 connections, 100,000 deliveries/s)
text:
5% of clients (56) periodically stop reading from their socket. Fast and stalled clients are
measured separately.

**With OS-default socket buffers** (stall 10 s every 30 s): **no server ever noticed.** Linux
auto-grows each socket's send buffer up to 4 MiB, so a 10 s stall (about 250 KB) sat in the kernel.
The stalled clients saw about 9.7 s delays and nothing was cut off. That's fine for correctness,
but it's a memory risk: 10,000 connections × 4 MiB is up to 40 GiB of kernel memory the server
never accounts for.

**With `SO_SNDBUF` capped at 64 KiB** (and a 16 KiB client receive window, stall 20 s every 30 s):

| | fast clients p50 / p99 | server cut-offs per run | clients complete | dup / gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Java, 1 dispatcher | 2.2 / 4.8 ms | 102 | 100% | 0 / 0 |
| Java, 2 dispatchers | 2.2 / 6.0 | 102 | 100% | 0 / 0 |
| Python, 1 process | 2.8 / 13.1 | 56 | 100% | 0 / 0 |
| Python, 2 processes | 2.3 / 7.8 | 57 | 100% | 0 / 0 |

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 5. Slow consumers and backpressure (1,000 connections, 100,000 deliveries/s)
text:
- **Fast clients are unaffected in every implementation.** The dispatch side only ever does a
  non-blocking offer, so a stalled client can't slow anyone else.
- Every stalled client was cut off when its 1,000-event queue overflowed, reconnected with its
  cursor, and replayed from the ring buffer: **0 lost, 0 duplicated**.
- **Where they diverge:** Java cut stalled clients off about twice as often (102 vs 56 per run).
  Its writer holds at most an 8 KiB buffer before blocking in `write()`. Python's writer appends a
  batch (up to 64 KiB) to the transport buffer and only then waits in `drain()`, whose high-water
  mark is another 64 KiB. So asyncio keeps about 100 KiB more per connection in user space and
  rides out more of each stall. Neither is "right": Java is stricter on memory, Python absorbs
  bursts longer. The difference comes from where each model puts its buffer, not from the queue
  size you configured.

title: asyncio vs Virtual Threads results: 6. What I'd conclude
text:
- For **correctness** there's no difference: same protocol, same audit, zero violations
  everywhere.
- **Latency at moderate load** is equal and dominated by Kafka (about 2 ms).
- **Scaling up**, the single event loop is the first thing to break (one core). Python needs a
  process per core, which also means a Kafka consumer per process. Java uses both cores from one
  process, but only once dispatch is spread across threads.
- **Memory**: Python is about 2× leaner per connection. Java needs deliberate buffer sizing to hold
  10k+ connections in 1 GiB.
- The biggest wins in this project came from **measuring, not from the language**: buffer sizes,
  kernel send buffers and dispatch parallelism each changed results by 10× or more.

title: RAG QA overview: Financial RAG QA
text:
[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Financial-RAG-QA/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Retrieval-augmented question answering over **FiQA-2018**: 57,638 answers from a
personal-finance Q&A forum, with **648 held-out questions** that people labelled for relevance.
Every answer sentence cites its passage, and every claim the system makes about itself is
measured: retrieval against the human labels (with confidence intervals and paired significance
tests), answer faithfulness with an LLM judge, and the judge itself against hand labels.

The measurement changed the design. The textbook pipeline (BM25 + embeddings + an off-the-shelf
cross-encoder) was **worse** than embeddings alone on this data; what worked was tuning fusion on
the dev split, fine-tuning the embedding model on FiQA's training questions, and fusing the
reranker's order with the retriever's instead of replacing it.

**Stack:** Python · PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector (HNSW) · bm25s · sentence-transformers (bge-base,
bge-reranker) · PyTorch (fine-tuning on Apple GPU) · Ollama (qwen3) or Groq · LangGraph · FastAPI
(SSE) · MCP · Docker Compose · GitHub Actions

title: RAG QA overview: Quick start
text:
Needs Docker, uv and, for answers, Ollama.

```bash
make install data infra        # deps, FiQA (~18 MB), Postgres + pgvector on :5436
uv run finrag train-embedder   # optional, 22 min on an Apple-silicon GPU; else the base model
make ingest                    # embed + load + HNSW, ~3 min
ollama pull qwen3:8b

```

uv run finrag ask "Is it better to pay off my mortgage early or invest?"
uv run finrag ask --agent "Can I deduct home office rent as an employee?"
curl -N -X POST localhost:8000/ask -H 'content-type: application/json' \

Unit tests use a hashing embedder, an overlap reranker and a scripted LLM, so CI needs no model

title: RAG QA overview: Data and licence
text: FiQA-2018 via BEIR (Maia et al., 2018). Code: MIT.

title: RAG QA design: Design
text:
Why each piece is the way it is, what else was considered, and where it stops working.
Numbers live in RESULTS.md.

title: RAG QA design: 1. The question this project answers
text:
"Does my RAG system work?" is two questions:

1. **Does retrieval find the right passages?** FiQA-2018 has human relevance judgments for 648
   test questions, so this is measured exactly (nDCG@10, MRR@10, recall@10/100). No LLM involved.
2. **Does the answer say only what those passages say?** There is no gold answer to compare
   against, so this needs a judge. The judge is an LLM, so the judge itself is measured against
   hand labels before any of its numbers are trusted.

Everything below serves one of those two measurements.

title: RAG QA design: 2. Dataset: FiQA-2018 (BEIR)
text:
57,638 answers from a personal-finance Q&A forum (StackExchange-style), 6,648 questions split
train/dev/test, test = 648 questions with 1,706 relevance judgments (about 2.6 relevant answers
per question).

Why FiQA: real user questions with messy wording ("Is it wise to..."), relevance labelled by
people, a standard BEIR benchmark so numbers can be compared with published ones (BM25 0.236
nDCG@10 in the BEIR paper), and small enough to embed on a laptop.

Known limits of the labels: only answers that the original asker's thread contained are marked
relevant, so a retrieved passage from another thread that answers the question equally well
counts as a miss. This **underestimates** every retriever, the strong ones most (they find more
of these unlabelled good passages). Reported numbers are therefore lower bounds and are only
compared with each other, on the same queries.

title: RAG QA design: 3. Storage: one PostgreSQL table
text:
```sql
docs(id, title, body,
     tsv       tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || body)) STORED,
     embedding vector(768))
-- HNSW (m=16, ef_construction=128, cosine) on embedding, GIN on tsv
```

**Why pgvector and not a vector database:** at 57k vectors (176 MB of float32) any store works.
Postgres means one system to run, transactions (the whole index is swapped atomically), real
SQL for looking at the data, and the text, the lexical index and the vectors in one row so a
hit never points at a missing document. A dedicated vector DB starts paying for itself at tens
of millions of vectors or when filtering + ANN need to scale out.

**Atomic reload:** `load_corpus` drops and recreates the table inside one transaction and builds
the indexes after the bulk `COPY ... FORMAT BINARY` (one index build is far faster than
maintaining HNSW row by row). If anything fails, the old index keeps serving. Tested by feeding
mismatched embeddings.

**HNSW vs exact:** pgvector's HNSW returns at most `ef_search` candidates, so `ef_search` is set
per transaction to at least `k` (the default 40 would silently cap a top-100 search at 40).
`finrag hnsw` measures recall@10 of HNSW against an exact scan (`enable_indexscan = off`) at
several `ef_search` values.

title: RAG QA design: 4. Retrievers
text:
| Variant | What it is | Why it is in the comparison |
|---|---|---|
| `bm25` | Okapi BM25 (k1=1.2, b=0.75), Snowball stemming, English stopwords, via `bm25s` | The lexical baseline every paper reports |
| `pg-fts` | Postgres `tsvector` + `ts_rank(..., 1)`, query lexemes OR-ed | To show that Postgres full-text search is **not** BM25 (no IDF) |
| `dense` | bge-base-en-v1.5 **fine-tuned on FiQA train**, cosine, HNSW | Semantic matching ("pay down debt" ~ "reduce loans") |
| `hybrid` | BM25 top-100 and dense top-100 fused with RRF (k=10, dense weighted 2x) | Lexical and semantic errors are different errors |
| `+rerank` | bge-reranker-base on the top 30, its order **fused** with the hybrid order (RRF, weight 0.5) | The default pipeline |
| `+rerank-only` | the same cross-encoder, its order alone | To show why fusion is needed |
| `+rerank-ft` | a cross-encoder fine-tuned on FiQA train, fused | Measured, not used (RESULTS.md) |

**Why BM25 lives outside Postgres:** `ts_rank` has no inverse document frequency, so "the" and
"amortization" weigh the same once matched. ParadeDB's `pg_search` adds real BM25 to Postgres but
is another extension to install; `bm25s` scores the whole corpus with sparse matrices in a few
milliseconds per query and its index is a few MB on disk.

title: RAG QA design: 4. Retrievers
text:
**Why `plainto_tsquery` is rewritten to OR:** it ANDs every word, and a 12-word question almost
never has all 12 words in one answer, so AND returns nothing for most queries. With OR, the
ranking function matters: `ts_rank_cd` (cover density) scored 0.037 nDCG@10 on dev because it
rewards long posts that repeat common words; `ts_rank` normalised by log length scored 0.190.

**bge query instruction:** bge v1.5 was trained with the prefix
`"Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "` on queries only. Leaving it off
or adding it to documents costs accuracy.

**Why RRF and not a weighted sum of scores:** BM25 scores are unbounded and their scale changes
per query; cosine similarities sit in a narrow band. Normalising them (min-max, z-score) is
fragile. RRF uses only ranks: `score(d) = Σ w/(k + rank)`. The paper's `k=60` with equal weights
made hybrid *worse* than dense alone here (BM25 is much weaker on FiQA); on dev, `k=10` with the
dense list weighted 2x was best. A small k makes the top ranks of each list count much more than
the rest, so a strong dense top 5 is not diluted by BM25's long tail.

title: RAG QA design: 4. Retrievers
text:
**Why the reranker's order is fused instead of trusted:** the off-the-shelf cross-encoder alone
was worse than the hybrid ranking it reordered (−14% on test), and worse the deeper it went.
It still carries signal the retrievers lack (it reads query and passage together), so its order
is fused with the hybrid order by RRF, cross-encoder weighted 0.5: +2.3% over hybrid (p=0.035).
Only the top 30 are rescored (one forward pass per pair, so cost is linear in depth); below
that the hybrid order is kept, so recall@100 does not change. Depth and weight chosen on dev.

title: RAG QA design: 4. Retrievers
text:
**Fine-tuning (finrag train-embedder / train-reranker):** both models are trained on FiQA's
train split (5,500 questions, 14,166 judged answers, disjoint from dev and test) with hard
negatives mined from this system's own hybrid retriever: highly ranked answers that are not
labelled relevant. The top 3 unjudged hits are skipped because FiQA's labels are incomplete and
the very top "negatives" are often relevant answers nobody labelled.
- *Embedder:* MultipleNegativesRankingLoss (each question's answer vs every other answer in the
  batch plus its hard negative), batch 32, with **GradCache** (cached MNRL, mini-batch 8): plain
  MNRL needed more than 12 GB of GPU memory at this batch size; GradCache computes the same loss
  in mini-batches. Batches never contain two answers to the same question (each would be
  trained as the other's negative). Result: recall@100 0.742 → 0.758 and the best hybrid; on its
  own, not significantly better (+1.8%, p=0.28).
- *Reranker:* binary cross-entropy on 52,666 pairs, positives weighted by the 2.7:1 negative
  ratio. Better than the off-the-shelf reranker on its own, but once the embedder was
  fine-tuned, stacking it lost to the off-the-shelf one fused (both learned from the same noisy
  labels). Kept as `+rerank-ft` for the comparison.
- *Apple-GPU specifics:* fp16 inference (3x faster); an `empty_cache` callback during training,
  because dynamic padding gives almost every batch a new shape and the MPS allocator kept every
  one (the process grew to 17 GB and swapped); eager attention for the embedder, because MPS
  `scaled_dot_product_attention` has no dropout support.

title: RAG QA design: 4. Retrievers
text:
**Tuning discipline:** every knob (RRF k, weights, depth, rerank depth and fusion weight, which
models to fine-tune and use) was chosen on the dev split (500 queries). The test split was run
once with the frozen configuration; the only later change was the pg-fts ranking function,
re-chosen on dev, which affects only that baseline row. Tuning on test would report a number the
system will not reproduce on new questions.

**Guard:** the index records which embedding model built it, and the dense retriever refuses to
run if the query model differs (query vectors from one model against document vectors from
another are silently meaningless).

title: RAG QA design: 5. Statistics
text:
Each metric is reported with a **95% bootstrap confidence interval** over queries (2,000
resamples), and every comparison has a **paired randomization test** (10,000 sign flips of the
per-query differences) plus win/loss counts. With 648 queries a 0.01 nDCG difference is often
noise; the p-value says which differences are real.

Per-query scores and TREC-format run files are written to `runs/`, so any number can be
recomputed (or checked with `trec_eval`) without rerunning retrieval.

title: RAG QA design: 6. Generation
text:
- Top 5 passages after reranking, each truncated to 220 words, numbered `[1]`..`[5]`.
- The prompt requires a citation on every sentence, forbids outside facts, and gives an exact
  abstention sentence for when the passages do not answer.
- The output is parsed into sentences with their citations. Citations to passages that do not
  exist (`[7]` when there are 5) are **flagged**, not silently dropped, and counted in results.
- An answer is "abstained" only if the abstention sentence is all it says. The model sometimes
  answers and *then* appends the abstention line; the first parser treated any occurrence as an
  abstention and threw the answer away. Now that line is removed from the judged sentences and
  the answer is flagged `hedged`.
- `temperature=0`, fixed seed; `think=false` for qwen3 (its default chain-of-thought adds
  hundreds of tokens of latency and leaks into the answer).

**Local by default:** Ollama with qwen3:8b on the laptop GPU, no API key, no rate limits, ₹0.
`LLM_PROVIDER=groq` switches to Groq's OpenAI-compatible API (Llama 3.3 70B) with 429 retry.
Both clients are plain `httpx`, so the whole contract (request body, streaming format, token
counts) is visible in `llm.py`.

title: RAG QA design: 7. Measuring faithfulness
text:
**Unit = sentence**, label = binary: "is everything this sentence claims stated or directly
implied by the passages it cites?" Binary sentence labels can be hand-labeled quickly and
consistently; a 1-10 "faithfulness score" cannot.

- Sentences with no citation, or only out-of-range citations, are unsupported **by rule** (no
  LLM call, and excluded from hand labeling since there is nothing to check).
- The judge sees only the cited passages, writes a short reason **before** its verdict (reasoning
  first improves accuracy; verdict-first lets the model rationalise), and returns JSON constrained
  by a schema.
- **Judge != generator.** qwen3:14b judges qwen3:8b. Same family is a known risk
  (self-preference); the hand labels are what measure whether it matters.

**Checking the judge:** `finrag label-sample` draws judged sentences **stratified** by verdict
(half supported, half not), because a judge that says "supported" 90% of the time would leave
almost no "not supported" cases to check. `finrag label` shows each sentence with its cited
passages in the terminal; `finrag agreement` reports raw agreement, Cohen's kappa, the confusion
matrix, the precision of each verdict, and agreement **re-weighted** to the judge's real verdict
mix (the stratified sample over-represents "not supported").

title: RAG QA design: 7. Measuring faithfulness
text:
**Objective cross-check that needs no judge:** FiQA's relevance labels say which passages are
good, so for every answer we also record whether its context contained a relevant passage and
whether it **cited** one.

title: RAG QA design: 8. The agent
text:
A LangGraph state machine:

```
plan -> retrieve -> grade --(follow-up query,  retrieve
                         \--(sufficient)--> answer -> verify -> END
```

- **plan:** rewrite the question into 1-3 searches. The original question always runs too, so
  rewriting can only add candidates, never lose the ones single-shot would have found.
- **retrieve:** hybrid+rerank per search, results fused with RRF, top 5 kept as evidence.
- **grade:** "is anything important missing? if so, one follow-up search". Capped at 2 rounds;
  a follow-up identical to an earlier search ends the loop.
- **answer:** the same prompt as single-shot, so differences come from evidence, not wording.
- **verify:** the generator checks its own sentences with the judge prompt and drops unsupported
  ones; if none survive, it abstains.
- Every LLM step degrades gracefully: unparseable planner/grader output falls back to
  single-shot behaviour, an unparseable self-check keeps the answer. Tested.

**Why LangGraph:** the control flow (a loop with an exit condition, then a linear tail) is
explicit and testable node by node; state is a typed dict. The nodes call this project's own
retriever and LLM client, not LangChain wrappers, so nothing is hidden.

title: RAG QA design: 8. The agent
text:
**Is it worth it?** Measured on the same 150 questions (RESULTS.md §5): faithfulness 0.81 →
0.94 (p < 0.001), at 4x the LLM calls and 3.7x the latency. The gain comes almost entirely from
the verify step (it dropped a sentence in 79 of 150 answers); query rewriting did not find
better evidence (relevant passage in context 64% vs 65%), and the grader asked for a follow-up
search on 4 of 150 questions. So the cheap version of the agent is "single-shot + verify"; the
planning and grading nodes are where to cut cost.

title: RAG QA design: 9. Serving
text:
- `GET /search`: any retrieval mode, with timings.
- `POST /ask`: **Server-Sent Events** — `passages` first (the UI shows sources immediately),
  then `token` deltas, then `done` with parsed citations, invalid citations and timings
  (retrieval, rerank, first token, total). Model errors become an `error` event instead of a
  silently closed stream.
- `POST /agent`: the agent with its trace.
- `GET /`: a one-file demo page that renders citations as they stream and flags invalid ones.
- **MCP server** (`finrag mcp`, stdio): `search_finance_qa` and `get_document` tools, so Claude
  Desktop, an IDE or another agent can use the retriever. Tested through a real MCP client
  session.

**Concurrency:** one process holds one Postgres connection and one copy of each model. PyTorch
modules and psycopg connections are not safe to share across threads, so retrieval is
serialised by a lock; token streaming, the slow part, runs outside it. Scaling out means more
processes (each with its own models) behind a load balancer, or moving embedding and reranking
to a batching inference server.

title: RAG QA design: 10. What I would do next
text:
- A larger reranker (bge-reranker-v2-m3) and listwise training for the in-domain one; a
  query-embedding cache.
- After the agent's verify step, a short rewrite so a dropped sentence never leaves the answer
  starting mid-thought.
- Serve the LLM on separate hardware: on one 24 GB laptop it pushes the retrieval models into
  swap (retrieval 85 ms alone, ~690 ms inside /ask).
- Judge with a stronger, different-family model (Llama 3.3 70B on Groq) and compare its
  agreement with the hand labels against qwen3:14b's.
- Chunking: FiQA answers are short (median ~90 words), so whole-document retrieval is fine here;
  long documents would need chunking with overlap and parent-document expansion.
- Filtered search (by date, source) with pgvector iterative scans.

title: RAG QA results: What the measurements changed
text:
The textbook pipeline is BM25 + embeddings + cross-encoder. Measured stage by stage on dev,
two of the three default choices made things worse:

title: RAG QA results: What the measurements changed
text:
1. **Equal-weight hybrid hurt.** BM25 is far weaker than the embeddings on FiQA (0.25 vs
   0.41): forum questions and answers rarely share exact words. With RRF k=60 and equal
   weights, fusion pulled the dense ranking *down* (dev, off-the-shelf embedder: 0.3722 vs
   0.4225 for dense alone).
   Tuned on dev (k=10, dense weighted 2×), hybrid adds a small significant gain.
2. **The off-the-shelf reranker hurt, badly** (−14% on test). bge-reranker-base was trained on
   web search and general QA, and FiQA's labels mean "an answer posted in that thread". On its
   own its order is worse than the retrieval it reorders, and the deeper it reranks the worse it
   gets (dev: 0.41 at depth 10 → 0.31 at depth 100).
3. **Fusing the reranker with the first-stage order fixed it.** RRF of the hybrid order and the
   cross-encoder order (cross-encoder weight 0.5) keeps both signals: +2.3% over hybrid on test.
4. **Fine-tuning helped where it was not obvious.** The fine-tuned embedder is not significantly
   better on its own (+1.8%, p=0.28) but raises recall@100 from 0.742 to 0.758, and the extra
   relevant answers it pulls into the candidate list are what hybrid fusion and reranking use.
5. **The fine-tuned reranker was not worth it.** It beat the off-the-shelf reranker when used
   alone (dev, off-the-shelf embedder, depth 10: 0.4232 vs 0.4109) but, stacked on the fine-tuned embedder, lost to the
   off-the-shelf one fused (dev 0.4353 vs 0.4447; test 0.4283 vs 0.4347, p=0.18). Both
   fine-tuned models learned from the same noisy labels; the off-the-shelf reranker adds a
   *different* signal. It is kept as `+rerank-ft` and measured, not used by default.

title: Fraud Detection design: Design
text: Why each piece is the way it is. Numbers live in RESULTS.md.

title: Fraud Detection design: 1. The data and what it can honestly tell us
text:
IEEE-CIS (Vesta, 2019): 590,540 labelled card-not-present transactions over 182 days, 3.5% fraud,
434 columns after joining the identity table. The column meanings are masked (C1-C14 are counts,
D1-D15 time deltas, V1-V339 Vesta's own engineered features), and the competition's test labels
were never published, so only the labelled half is used and the project carves its own validation
and test periods out of it.

`TransactionDT` is seconds from an unpublished reference point. Day 1 to 182 is all we know; the
hour of day is derived assuming the reference is midnight (the hourly fraud pattern supports it,
but it is an assumption).

title: Fraud Detection design: 2. Split by time, not at random
text:
| set | days | rows | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| train | 1-119 | 410,601 | fit models, fit category codes |
| validation | 120-151 | 90,613 | early stopping, Optuna, calibration, threshold |
| test | 152-182 | 89,326 | touched once per model, for the numbers we report |

A fraud model is always trained on the past and used on the future. A random split lets the
model see a card's next-week transactions while training, which a deployed model never can.
`fraudops leakage` measures the gap instead of asserting it. Cuts fall on whole days so one day
never straddles two sets.

The validation month is used for several decisions (early stopping, 30 Optuna trials, the
isotonic calibrator, the cost threshold), so validation scores are optimistic. That is what the
untouched test month is for.

title: Fraud Detection design: 3. Features: only the past
text:
**Reconstructed customer.** There is no customer id. `D1` is "days since the card was first
seen", so `day - D1` is a constant per account: the account's start day. `uid = card1 + addr1 +
account start` is the standard reconstruction from the competition's top solutions. It is a
proxy, not ground truth; 11% of rows have no `addr1` or `D1` and get no uid features.

**History per entity** (`card1` and `uid`): number of earlier transactions, their mean and
standard deviation of amount, this amount divided by that mean, seconds since the previous one,
and how many arrived in the last 24 hours. "Earlier" means strictly before in stream order
`(TransactionDT, TransactionID)`. It never includes the row itself or anything after it.

Many public notebooks compute these aggregates over train+test at once (group mean over the whole
table, frequency encoding over everything). That leaks the future into the past. The `global`
mode exists only so the leakage experiment can measure how much it inflates scores.

title: Fraud Detection design: 3. Features: only the past
text:
**Known fraud, with the label delay modelled.** For each card and uid: how many earlier
transactions have a *matured* label, how many of those were fraud, and the rate. A label matures
`LABEL_DELAY_DAYS` (30) after the transaction, because that is roughly when a chargeback has
arrived. A transaction younger than that is *unknown*, not legitimate. Labelling a fresh
transaction "not fraud" just because no chargeback has come yet is the classic way this feature
leaks. `fraudops label-delay` reruns the model with labels usable after 7, 30, 60 and 90 days:
the price of a slow chargeback feed.

Vesta labelled later transactions linked to a charged-back card (same account, email or billing address) as fraud too (the competition host explained this in the Kaggle data discussion
thread), which is why account-level fraud history is so predictive here. In a real
issuer the same thing happens operationally: a compromised account keeps getting hit until it is
blocked.

title: Fraud Detection design: 3. Features: only the past
text:
**A feature that was a date in disguise.** The first version used `account_start` (day - D1) as
a model input. The drift check put it at PSI 1.84 between train and test, the worst of all 450
columns, and SHAP had it second most important. It is a calendar date: test-month accounts have
start days the model never saw. Dropping it alone made validation *worse* (0.665 to 0.649): it was
helping by letting the model recognise accounts that had committed fraud in training, i.e.
standing in for past labels. Once the honest known-fraud features existed, validation preferred
the model without it, so it is now used only to build the uid. All three decisions were made on
validation, not test.

Raw `TransactionDT` and `day` are excluded for the same reason: a time trend learnt on days
1-119 extrapolates nonsense onto day 160.

**Categoricals:** codes learnt on train only. Values seen fewer than 20 times, and values never
seen, share one "rare" code; missing stays missing (LightGBM learns which side missing values
go). Unseen values in production are normal (new email domains, new devices), so this path is
exercised in tests.

title: Fraud Detection design: 4. One definition, two implementations, one test
text:
The offline builder is vectorised Polars (window functions plus a sorted `searchsorted` for the
24-hour counts) because it has to process 590k rows in about a second. The API cannot run window
functions over a table, so `OnlineFeatureStore` keeps a small running state per entity (count,
sum, sum of squares, last timestamp, a deque of the last day's timestamps) and reads it before
adding the new transaction.

Two implementations of one definition is how training/serving skew happens. The guard is a
replay: push every transaction through the online store in stream order and compare every value
with the offline column. Both sides do the same float64 arithmetic in the same order and round
through float32 the same way, so the comparison is exact equality, not a tolerance. The test runs
in CI on synthetic data; the full 590k-row replay was run on the real data (RESULTS.md).

The benchmark then goes one level further: the real HTTP API, warmed with train+val history,
scores test transactions in order, and every returned probability is compared with the offline
batch prediction for the same row.

title: Fraud Detection design: 5. Models
text:
* **Logistic regression** on the ~100 non-Vesta columns (median impute + missing indicators,
  rank scaling with `QuantileTransformer`, one-hot categoricals). The first version used
  `StandardScaler` and its test PR-AUC was half its validation PR-AUC (0.17 vs 0.35; recall at 1%
  FPR fell to 2%): counts and time deltas in the test month sit far outside the training range,
  and a linear model extrapolates them without limit. Rank scaling caps every input at the
  training distribution's tails. Trees never had the problem; they only split.
* **LightGBM** with hand-picked settings, then the **same model without each engineered family**
  (velocity/history, known fraud, both: are they worth their serving cost?), then an **Optuna** search (TPE, 30 trials,
  early stopping on validation PR-AUC, median pruning of hopeless trials; the hand-picked
  setting is enqueued as trial 0 so the search must beat it).

**Metric: PR-AUC (average precision)**, not ROC-AUC. With 3.5% positives, ROC-AUC is dominated by
the easy negatives; precision-recall reflects what a fraud team sees. Also reported: recall at
1% false-positive rate. The tuned-vs-logistic gap gets a paired bootstrap interval over test rows.

title: Fraud Detection design: 6. From a score to a decision
text:
A model ranks; the business needs approve or review. Costs (assumptions, in `config.Costs`): a
review costs $10 (analyst time plus friction for a good customer); a missed fraud costs its amount
plus a $20 chargeback fee. Compared on the test month:

1. flag nothing (the cost of having no model),
2. the naive `score >= 0.5`,
3. the single threshold that minimised cost on validation (exact search over every distinct
   score),
4. the **expected-cost rule**: review when `p * (amount + fee) > review cost`. A $2,000
   transaction at 1% risk is worth reviewing; a $5 one at 30% is not. This needs a probability
   that means what it says, hence:

**Calibration.** LightGBM scores are ranks, not probabilities. An isotonic regression fitted on
validation maps them to probabilities; RESULTS.md shows predicted vs observed fraud by decile on
the test month. Ranking metrics are computed on the raw score (isotonic steps create ties).

title: Fraud Detection design: 7. Explanations
text:
Every API response carries the top five features by TreeSHAP contribution (log-odds). LightGBM
computes exact TreeSHAP natively (`pred_contrib=True`), so serving needs no `shap` dependency; a
test checks the values equal `shap.TreeExplainer` and that contributions sum to the model's
margin. The global top-20 is the mean absolute contribution on 20k test rows.

title: Fraud Detection design: 8. MLflow registry: champion and challenger
text:
Each `train` logs runs (params, metrics, results JSON) to a local SQLite-backed MLflow and
registers the tuned model as a new version of `fraud-detector`. The deployable artifact is one
pyfunc wrapping the whole bundle (category codes, feature order, booster, calibrator, cost
rule), so the API serves exactly what was evaluated. A new version takes the `champion` alias
only if its validation PR-AUC beats the current champion's; otherwise it is tagged
`challenger`. The API loads `models:/fraud-detector@champion`.

title: Fraud Detection design: 9. Serving
text:
FastAPI, one transaction per request: online features, encode, predict, decide, explain, then
add the transaction to the store. `POST /v1/chargeback` reports a fraud; the store holds each
entity's last 30 days of transactions in a pending queue and, when one passes the delay, counts
it as fraud if a chargeback was reported and as legitimate otherwise. (A chargeback that arrives
after the delay is missed; the 30-day assumption is exactly that.) The handler is sync, so FastAPI runs it in a worker thread and
the event loop stays free. The store has a lock; with several workers each process would need a
shared store (Redis, keyed by entity), which is the obvious next step and out of scope.
Single-row LightGBM prediction runs with one thread: threading overhead outweighs the work.

title: Fraud Detection design: 10. Drift
text:
PSI per feature (bins at the training deciles, missing as its own bin) for each week after
training, on the 30 features the model relies on most, plus PSI of the score itself and the
weekly fraud rate and PR-AUC. Labels arrive late in reality, so score PSI and feature PSI are the
early warning; PR-AUC is the lagging truth.

title: Fraud Detection design: 11. Laptop budget
text:
24 GB unified memory, shared with everything else: float32 storage, models capped at 4 threads,
heavy steps under `nice`. No Docker for this project.

title: Fraud Detection results: 2. Models on the test month (`fraudops train`)
text:
* **Tuned LightGBM vs logistic:** +0.116 test PR-AUC, paired bootstrap 95% CI **+0.105 to
  +0.128** (300 resamples of test rows).
* **What the features are worth:** the known-fraud features (30-day label delay) carry the gain:
  removing them costs 0.093 test PR-AUC. The velocity/history features (counts, mean amount,
  time since previous, 24-hour activity) add only 0.002: Vesta's 339 V columns and the C counts
  already encode most of that. They stay because they cost under a millisecond to serve, but
  this is the honest result.
* **Optuna:** 30 trials in 8.3 minutes, 20 pruned early by the median rule. Best validation
  PR-AUC 0.7172 vs 0.7167 for the hand-picked setting (enqueued as trial 0). Tuning barely
  matters here; the features do.
* **Val to test gap** (0.717 to 0.644): validation was used for early stopping, tuning,
  calibration and the threshold, and test is further from training in time. Section 7 shows the
  decay week by week.

**First-version numbers kept for the record** (registry v1, now `retired`): test PR-AUC 0.568
with `account_start` as an input and no known-fraud features; logistic with `StandardScaler`
0.166 test vs 0.347 validation (recall at 1% FPR 2.2%). DESIGN.md section 3 and 5 explain both.

title: Fraud Detection results: 3. From score to decision (`fraudops train`, test month)
text:
Costs: a review $10; a missed fraud = amount + $20 chargeback fee. Fraud in the test month: $540k
of cost if nothing is flagged.

| rule (all chosen on validation) | cost | saved vs no model | flagged | precision | recall | fraud $ caught |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| flag nothing | $539,636 | 0% | 0% | - | 0% | 0% |
| raw score ≥ 0.5 | $356,551 | 33.9% | 1.9% | 84.2% | 46.3% | 35.9% |
| best single threshold on validation | $209,753 | 61.1% | 11.8% | 23.8% | 80.4% | 80.7% |
| **expected cost: review if p × (amount + $20) > $10** | **$169,886** | **68.5%** | **9.0%** | **27.5%** | **70.9%** | **85.0%** |

The expected-cost rule catches *fewer* frauds than the best threshold (70.9% vs 80.4%) but more
fraud **dollars** (85.0% vs 80.7%) with fewer reviews (9.0% vs 11.8%): it spends reviews on
large transactions and lets small low-risk ones through. On validation it saves 74.1%.

Fraud Detection results: 4. Leakage, measured (`fraudops leakage`)
text:
Same LightGBM settings throughout, test PR-AUC:

| | time split (train past, test future) | random split |
|---|---|---|
| past-only features (production-like) | **0.637** | 0.873 |
| future-peeking aggregates (whole-table group stats) | 0.641 | 0.887 |

A random split overstates the model by 37% (0.637 to 0.873): the same cards' later transactions
sit in training. The future-peeking aggregates add little on top here, so the split is where
the leak bites in this dataset.

title: Fraud Detection results: 5. What a faster chargeback feed is worth (`fraudops label-delay`)
text:
Known-fraud features with labels usable after N days, same model settings:

| label delay | 7 days | 30 days (used) | 60 days | 90 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| val PR-AUC | 0.759 | 0.717 | 0.683 | 0.645 |
| test PR-AUC | **0.707** | 0.637 | 0.607 | 0.573 |

Every month of label delay costs about 0.03-0.07 PR-AUC. At 90 days the known-fraud features are
worth little more than nothing (0.573 vs 0.551 without them). Getting chargebacks or fraud
confirmations faster is worth as much as any modelling change in this project.

title: Fraud Detection results: 6. Serving (`fraudops build-store`, `fraudops bench`)
text:
**Feature parity.** The online store replayed all 590,540 transactions (with chargebacks reported
after scoring) and reproduced the offline value of every one of 24 online-computed columns:
**14,172,960 values, 0 mismatches** (exact equality, 6.2 s). The same test runs in CI on
synthetic data.

**Store snapshot** at the end of validation: 501,214 transactions replayed in 4.5 s; 12,914 cards
and 175,045 uids; 21.6 MB.

**HTTP benchmark:** uvicorn with the registry champion and that snapshot; the first 5,200 test
transactions sent one at a time in stream order (first 200 dropped as warm-up); fraud rows
reported through `/v1/chargeback` after scoring.

| | client p50 | client p95 | client p99 | server p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| with top-5 SHAP reasons | 7.9 ms | **8.2 ms** | 8.3 ms | 7.6 ms |
| without reasons | 1.0 ms | **1.1 ms** | 1.2 ms | 0.7 ms |

Every one of the 5,000 API probabilities equals the offline batch prediction for the same row
(max absolute difference 0.0). The review rate in this slice is 7.8%. Explanations cost about
7 ms: TreeSHAP walks every path of 605 trees over 453 features. A real deployment would explain
only the transactions it sends to review (9%).

title: Fraud Detection results: 7. Drift and decay (`fraudops drift`)
Fraud Detection results: 7. Drift and decay (`fraudops drift`)
text:
* **The score never drifted** (PSI 0.06-0.11, under the 0.2 alarm every week) **while PR-AUC fell
  from 0.81 to 0.56-0.67.** Input and score monitoring alone would have reported "stable".
  Performance monitoring on matured labels is what catches decay, and it lags by the label
  delay. That is the argument for a scheduled retrain rather than a drift-triggered one.
* 25 of 453 features exceed PSI 0.2 between train and val+test. The worst is
  `card1_fraud_rate_known` (1.34), and that drift is structural: in the first 30 days of
  training no label has matured yet, so the feature is missing there. Next: start training at
  day 31 so the feature is populated for every training row. Real drift: `id_31` (browser and
  version, 0.36) as new browser versions ship; the M1-M9 match flags (0.30-0.32) change their
  missing rate.

[](https://github.com/AnuragBhandary/Product-Analytics-AB-Testing/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**Dashboard:** https://anuragbhandary.github.io/Product-Analytics-AB-Testing/

Two questions about one online store: what do customers do, and can you trust an A/B test?

1. **Product analytics on GA4.** Google's public GA4 ecommerce export (4.3M events, 270k users)
   modelled in **BigQuery with dbt**: sessions, checkout funnel, weekly retention cohorts,
   channels and products. The tests reconcile revenue to the cent against an independent
   deduplication of the raw events.
2. **Experimentation.** A statistics toolkit (SRM, power, CUPED/CUPAC, delta method,
   sequential tests, multiple testing, doubly robust estimation). It is validated by thousands
   of simulated experiments on real GA4 users, then used to read out a **real 14M-user
   randomised experiment** (Criteo's incrementality test).

**Stack:** BigQuery · dbt · SQL · Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, DuckDB) · Evidence ·
Power BI (DAX) · GitHub Actions + Pages
